title: Dominguez gets nod for second term at IMO helm
summary: Arsenio Dominguez is poised for a second term as IMO Secretary-General, extending his leadership until 2031 amidst ongoing climate inaction. His initial tenure saw the "Net-Zero Framework" and critical emissions pricing mechanisms suffer significant delays due to member state divisions. This re-appointment offers little confidence that the IMO will finally enforce the stringent regulations necessary to genuinely curb maritime carbon intensity.
content:
Arsenio Dominguez is set to remain at the helm of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) until the end of 2031 after the UN shipping agency’s Council backed his appointment for another four-year term.

The 40-member Council endorsed the Panamanian’s extension during its 138th session in London, with the decision still requiring formal approval from the IMO Assembly when it meets in late 2027.

If approved, Dominguez will serve a second term from January 1, 2028, to December 31, 2031, extending his leadership of the world’s maritime regulator during a period of mounting challenges over shipping decarbonisation and maritime security.

Dominguez, who took office in January 2024, has spent much of his first term navigating increasingly divided positions among member states over the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework, which aims to introduce a global marine fuel standard and emissions pricing mechanism.

The framework, agreed in principle in April 2025, suffered a major setback last October when governments voted to delay its adoption by a year following strong opposition led by the United States and Saudi Arabia.

Efforts to revive the agreement have continued throughout 2026, with negotiations set to culminate in another critical round of talks later this month. The Marine Environment Protection Committee meets from November 30 to December 3, followed by a planned extraordinary session on December 4 to revisit the framework’s adoption.

The IMO has also faced mounting pressure over the safety of commercial shipping amid continuing attacks and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Black Sea, issues that feature on the agenda of this week’s Council meeting.

Dominguez, the IMO’s tenth secretary-general, previously served as director of its Marine Environment Division, administrative director and chief of staff. He also represented Panama at the organisation and chaired its Marine Environment Protection Committee.

He succeeded South Korea’s Kitack Lim in January 2024 after securing the Council’s backing in July 2023 and subsequent Assembly approval.

title: Manned brain, unmanned muscle: ST Engineering's MRV makes its European debut
summary: ST Engineering's new 150-metre, 8,000-tonne Multi-Role Vessel (MRV) concept makes its European debut, boasting a 7,000 nautical mile range for naval operations. Conspicuously absent from the presentation are any details regarding the vessel's fuel type, consumption, or projected CO2 emissions. For a platform of this size and intended extended deployment, transparency on its environmental impact is crucial, regardless of its military designation.
content:
The Singaporean group presents its MRV unmanned-systems mothership concept in Paris, betting that Manned-Unmanned Teaming is the answer for navies seeking greater operational reach with fewer sailors

ST Engineering’s Multi-Role Vessel (MRV) makes its European debut at Euronaval 2026, which runs from 3 to 6 November at Paris Nord Villepinte. Presented as a scale model, the vessel embodies a proposition centred on distributed Manned-Unmanned Teaming (MUM-T): a crewed mothership designed to deploy and coordinate unmanned systems, extending a navy’s surveillance capabilities, maritime presence and operational reach.

Where a conventional corvette or frigate is optimised primarily around its own sensors and weapons, the MRV is conceived from the outset as a mothership and command hub. Rather than serving simply as a transport for unmanned craft, it is intended to remain the manned command-and-control platform of a wider force package, directing and coordinating multiple unmanned systems while they undertake missions at sea.

A substantial platform with extended reach

The MRV is designed around a substantial hull measuring 150 metres in length, with a beam of 21 metres, a draft of 6 metres, and a displacement of 8,000 tonnes. Its maximum speed is 22 knots, while its stated range of 7,000 nautical miles underline its intended suitability for sustained maritime operations.

These characteristics provide the platform with the endurance and capacity required to operate as a forward-deployed command centre, supporting unmanned assets over extended distances while retaining the ability to operate independently as a manned vessel.

The centrepiece of the concept is the vessel’s stern launch system, from which unmanned surface vessels (USVs) are deployed. Once at sea, these offboard assets are intended to undertake missions such as surveillance, reconnaissance and threat investigation, while the MRV remains the manned command-and-control hub orchestrating their activities. The arrangement keeps sailors concentrated on command, decision-making and coordination while extending the force’s reach across the maritime domain.

Manned-Unmanned Teaming at the heart of the concept

The principle underpinning the MRV is MUM-T. Rather than treating drones and unmanned craft as supplementary equipment bolted onto a conventional fighting ship, the MRV treats them as an organic, distributed force package.

The unmanned systems extend the vessel’s surveillance and operational reach, contribute additional information to the maritime picture and potentially operate in areas where deploying a crewed platform would be less desirable. The manned element remains the decision-making core, retaining command authority while coordinating the activities of multiple autonomous or remotely operated assets.

According to ST Engineering, the result is a force package in which manned platforms and autonomous systems operate as a cohesive whole, extending operational reach, enhancing situational awareness and improving mission effectiveness.

Advanced sensors and weapons

Although the MRV is conceived primarily as a mothership for unmanned systems, its combat architecture also incorporates a substantial suite of sensors and weapons, allowing it to retain independent defensive and operational capabilities.

The vessel’s sensor and cyber architecture includes electro-optical systems, fire-control radar and cybersecurity capabilities. These are complemented by a multifunction radar based on fixed-panel, electronically steered technology, intended to support the vessel’s surveillance and engagement requirements.

Its proposed armament encompasses several layers of defensive and offensive capability.

For air defence, the MRV is equipped with surface-to-air missile systems including MBDA’s MICA and Aster, providing engagement capabilities against aerial threats. A dedicated surface-to-surface missile system adds an offensive capability against surface targets.

The vessel’s gun armament includes a Leonardo 76 mm Strales gun, designed to provide precision engagement capability, together with a 30 mm MK30-C30 remotely controlled weapon system, adding another layer of close-range defence and engagement capability.

The combination of advanced sensors, missile systems and gun armament suggests that the MRV is not intended to be merely a passive support vessel. Its combat systems are designed to complement its mothership role, providing protection and the ability to contribute directly to naval operations.

From Singaporean experience to European ambitions

The MRV does not arrive in Paris from a standing start. ST Engineering’s unmanned credentials are already established in service.

The Venus family of USVs operates with the Republic of Singapore Navy (RSN), while in May 2025 the group secured a contract to supply the service with a complete unmanned mine-countermeasures suite comprising surface vessels, autonomous underwater vehicles and the mission management system that integrates them.

This experience provides an important foundation for the MRV concept. The challenge is no longer simply developing individual unmanned platforms, but integrating them into a coherent operational architecture in which multiple systems can be deployed, coordinated and managed from a single manned vessel.

The RSN’s own fleet of six Multi-Role Combat Vessels represents a separate national programme involving larger vessels measuring 150 metres in length and displacing 8,000 tonnes, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2028. This programme applies the mothership doctrine at fleet scale, although it should not be confused with the MRV concept presented by ST Engineering at Euronaval.

A proposition for European navies

For European and allied navies weighing how to build distributed maritime capability, the MRV’s debut is therefore less a conventional platform presentation than an offer of a complete approach to MUM-T operations.

The concept addresses several pressures confronting modern naval forces: the need to extend surveillance and operational reach, the growing importance of autonomous systems, the increasing cost of maintaining large crewed fleets and the requirement to operate across increasingly complex maritime environments.

By combining a substantial manned platform, advanced combat systems and the capacity to deploy and coordinate unmanned assets, ST Engineering is proposing a different way of organising naval power.

The MRV’s central proposition is straightforward: the future fleet may not need every platform to carry every capability. Instead, a manned command vessel could coordinate a distributed network of unmanned systems, multiplying the effect of its crew and extending the reach of the force.

For ST Engineering, Euronaval 2026 offers an opportunity to bring that proposition before European decision-makers. Whether the MRV ultimately attracts international customers will depend on operational requirements, procurement priorities and the ability to demonstrate the effectiveness of its integrated manned-unmanned architecture. But its European debut signals that the debate over the future of naval warfare is increasingly shifting from individual ships towards the coordinated combat systems they can command.

title: Ammonia-Powered Bulk Carrier Takes on Green Fuel in Australian First
summary: Fortescue and CMB.TECH announced Australia's first ammonia bunkering for the bulk carrier Mineral Europa, presenting it as a 'green' milestone. However, actual decarbonization hinges entirely on ammonia's production method and strict control of potent nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions during combustion. Without verifiable lifecycle emissions data, this operation remains a bunkering trial, not proven progress against carbon intensity targets or FuelEU Maritime obligations.
content:
Australia has completed its first green ammonia bunkering operation involving an ammonia-powered bulk carrier, marking another step toward bringing alternative fuels into commercial shipping.

The operation took place earlier this week at the Port of Port Hedland in Western Australia, where the 300-meter Mineral Europa received certified green ammonia from a bunker vessel before entering port to load iron ore bound for China.

The vessel, described as the world’s first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, is operated by CMB.TECH and chartered to Australian mining giant Fortescue.

According to a joint announcement from Fortescue, Pilbara Ports and CMB.TECH, the ship-to-ship transfer took approximately two hours and was completed successfully at 8:42 a.m. local time.

The operation required extensive planning, including vessel compatibility assessments, ammonia dispersion modeling, emergency response procedures, and additional marine support. Port authorities said the trial proceeded only after all safety and operational requirements had been met.

The successful bunkering is particularly significant for the iron ore trade, which relies heavily on large bulk carriers transporting Australian exports to Asian steelmakers. Fortescue is seeking to reduce emissions from those voyages by introducing ammonia-powered vessels and developing a reliable supply of green marine fuel.

Unlike conventional marine fuels, ammonia contains no carbon and produces no carbon dioxide when used as fuel. Its overall emissions benefits, however, depend on how it is produced and on controlling other emissions, including nitrous oxide. Ammonia’s toxicity also presents additional challenges for ship operators, ports and bunker suppliers.

Fortescue Metals CEO Dino Otranto said the operation demonstrated that ammonia bunkering is moving beyond small-scale testing toward practical use in major commercial ports.

“Industry has moved ahead of regulation to prove the technology,” Otranto said.

He added that policy certainty and long-term fuel purchasing commitments would be needed to support further investment in green ammonia production and bunkering infrastructure.

Fortescue has been an early supporter of ammonia as a marine fuel. In 2024, its Fortescue Green Pioneer completed ammonia-fueled propulsion trials in Singapore, demonstrating the technology aboard a converted offshore support vessel.

The company has since expanded its commercial shipping ambitions through a partnership with CMB.TECH. In addition to Mineral Europa, Fortescue charters nine other vessels from the shipping group that can be converted to operate on ammonia in the future. The companies also announced an agreement earlier this year covering up to 12 ammonia-capable bulk carriers.

The Port Hedland operation builds on an earlier ship-to-ship ammonia transfer trial at nearby Dampier in September 2024, which helped establish procedures for handling ammonia between vessels.

Pilbara Ports is now studying the development of a clean fuel bunkering hub in the region, with the latest trial expected to inform future operations.

While ammonia-powered shipping still faces substantial hurdles involving fuel cost, availability, safety and regulatory standards, the Port Hedland operation demonstrates how the fuel could be supplied to large commercial vessels at one of the world’s busiest bulk export ports.

The companies did not disclose the quantity of green ammonia transferred during the operation.

title: NAPA on why wind-assisted ships need proof of savings, not just a contract
summary: While BIMCO offers new contractual frameworks for sharing wind-assisted propulsion savings, NAPA correctly identifies a critical flaw: verifiable proof of actual fuel reduction. Claims of 5-20% fuel savings remain unsubstantiated without robust data isolating wind's true contribution from other voyage factors. Until shipowners provide transparent, voyage-specific proof, these systems offer no guaranteed relief from FuelEU Maritime fines or improved CII ratings.
content:
BIMCO recently adopted its Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum in Autumn 2026, giving owners and charterers a contractual framework to agree how the cost, time and fuel savings of a retrofit are shared during a time charter. For wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS), it targets the obstacle most often cited for slow uptake: the owner usually pays for the installation while the charterer keeps the fuel savings.

A contract for sharing savings, however, only works if both parties can agree on what the savings were. That is where wind-assisted shipping still has a gap.

Wind propulsion has moved well past the trial stage. According to the International Windship Association, more than 100 commercial ships now sail with wind propulsion fitted, totalling over six million deadweight tonnes, and around 100 more are on order. Retrofits are typically saving between 5% – 20% of fuel in service, with the variation dependent on trade route, prevailing winds and the size of the sails relative to the ship’s installed power. That spread is the commercial problem in a single figure: on any given voyage, how much of the saving came from the sails, and how much from good weather or a well-chosen route?

Those numbers matter more each year as CII, FuelEU Maritime and the EU ETS raise the bar on efficiency and emissions. FuelEU Maritime already rewards wind directly, applying a multiplier to a vessel’s GHG intensity that is banded according to available effective wind power relative to propulsion power. The IMO Net-Zero Framework, which is still under discussion at the time of writing, would pair a fuel standard with emissions pricing and could have a similar impact worldwide. Knowing how much a WAPS contributes to a ship’s emissions profile is therefore part of knowing a fleet’s compliance exposure.

Routing is a large part of the answer. For a conventional ship, wind is mostly an obstacle that adds resistance, rough seas and fuel burn. For a ship with rotor sails or wing-sails, it becomes a possible source of thrust, which can justify a longer track to reach a better wind speed and angle, or a slower passage to get more out of the sails. The best route will vary with the optimization objective, such as fuel saving, speed, arrival time, cost or profit, as well as with the weather, the ship and its wind system.

Many weather routing tools were never built to do this. They treat the vessel’s performance as fixed and add wind as a simple extra push, rather than modelling how it interacts with waves, rudder angle, propeller and engine load at the same time. A credible approach maps wind along the whole route before departure, reassesses it against swell, wind waves and current, and states savings in dollars rather than percentages, so operators can see the financial case for a routing decision before committing to it.

NAPA’s performance models start from the ship’s 3D hull form and hydrodynamics and are calibrated with operational data. That allows them to estimate what the vessel would have burned on the same voyage, in the same conditions, with no sails. This counterfactual baseline is what turns a claimed saving into a verifiable one – and it is the figure an owner and a charterer need in front of them when they divide the savings under a charter. The same model supports pre-installation simulation, routing in service and post-installation validation.

The same evidence matters for compliance. FuelEU Maritime already rewards wind directly, applying a multiplier to a vessel’s GHG intensity that is banded according to available effective wind power relative to propulsion power. Under the EU ETS, every tonne of CO2 the sails avoid is an allowance the company does not have to surrender. The IMO Net-Zero Framework, which is still under discussion at the time of writing, would pair a fuel standard with emissions pricing and could have a similar impact worldwide. Knowing how much a WAPS contributes to a ship’s emissions profile is therefore part of knowing a fleet’s compliance exposure, not only its fuel bill.

It also helps with the split incentive. Under time charters, the owner usually pays for the installation, and the charterer keeps the fuel savings, which is widely seen as the biggest structural obstacle to wider uptake. Voyage-level data that isolates the WAPS contribution from gains due to routing or weather gives both parties evidence to negotiate how savings are divided.

Verification has limits, wind forecasts can shift quickly, so a route planned on a five-day forecast may lose its advantage as conditions change. Predicting sail performance in heavy seas is harder than in settled weather. And no model closes the distance between what a ship could theoretically achieve and what a crew, bound by schedule and charterer instructions, can realistically deliver.

title: Australia approves seabed site where a Japanese company will store carbon pollution
summary: Australia has approved a seabed site for a Japanese company to store 443 million tonnes of CO2, pushing a carbon capture technology widely seen as a distraction. While proponents suggest this contested solution aids sectors like shipping, the IEA projects it will contribute less than 5% of emission reductions by 2050. Such speculative projects risk diverting focus from the urgent need for immediate, measurable reductions in vessel emissions and improved CII performance.
content:
Australia has designated a seabed storage site near its northern coast where a Japanese company plans to store massive amounts of carbon pollution using a technology that has divided climate scientists.

Approval of the site to store up to 443 million metric tons (488 million tons) of carbon dioxide has become part of the global debate over carbon capture and storage: Proponents say the project will play an important role in reducing emissions from hard-to-clean-up industries like steel production and shipping. Critics say it will harm critical habitats and endangered wildlife while promoting a technology that prolongs the use of heavily polluting fossil fuels.

Carbon capture remains a contested climate solution

Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, is a three-step process that captures, transports and stores CO2, which contributes to climate change when released in the atmosphere.

Some governments and fossil fuel giants including Exxon Mobil and Shell promote the strategy as a climate solution that buys time for countries and industries to transition to cleaner energy.

While the International Energy Agency considers carbon capture, utilization and storage a tool for curbing climate change, the agency’s net-zero emissions scenario forecasts it will contribute less than 5% of emission reductions by 2050.

Detractors say it will slow progress of already off-track global efforts to curb emissions and allow power plants and industrial facilities to continue burning fossil fuels under the promise of capturing the exhaust later.

CCS projects are moving ahead: The United States has several in operation and the European Union’s first offshore facility opened in September.

Australia's project would be led by Japanese energy company Inpex, which is conducting environmental impact assessments and must obtain other government licenses before a final decision is made and CO2 injection starts.

The project would start in Darwin, the Northern Territory capital city on the Timor Sea, and would extend 260 kilometers (162 miles) offshore, injecting CO2 into a deep saline aquifer called West Peron.

Inpex says the primary customer would be the nearby Ichthys liquefied natural gas facility, which is majority-owned by Inpex and which exports a majority of its gas to Japan.

Other companies in the future could store their CO2 at the site, which can permanently store up to 443 million metric tons (488 million tons) of CO2 over 35 years, according to Inpex.

The government welcomes the project, while environmentalists reject it

Australian Resources Minister Madeleine King said the designation of the site was an important step and demonstrated the government's support for technologies that help reduce emissions.

“Carbon capture and storage will play an important role in reducing emissions from hard-to-abate industries, supporting Australia’s transition to net zero,” King said in a statement.

King and Australia's Department of Industry, Science and Resources did not respond to an email from AP seeking further comment.

Environmental groups are concerned about the impact the project would have on marine, coastal and terrestrial ecosystems. The area overlaps with habitats for multiple threatened and migratory species, including dugongs, turtles and seabirds.

Construction of the project will be a major disturbance these ecosystems, said Chelsea Deng, a campaigner at the Australian Marine Conservation Society.

“A lot of it involves dredging, drilling, piling into the ocean,” she said. "It causes sediment disturbance. It causes water quality pollution through the chemical discharge. There’s a lot of underwater noise as part of it.”

Once the project is in operation there will be more marine traffic in the area, causing further disruptions, and routine underwater surveys the company will do to check for leaks will further harm the ecosystem, she said.

“This is really impactful and harmful to whales particularly, but it can negatively impact anything from plankton which have been shown to die up to 1.2 kilometers (3/4 miles) away from these seismic impulses,” she said “And this goes on for decades while this project is underway, because they have to continually monitor these CO2 plumes that they’re injecting underground.”

Inpex did not respond to an email from The Associated Press asking for comment.

Japan says CCS is essential to meet its own climate goals

Japan — one of the world's top polluters — has ambitious goals to reduce its carbon emissions by 60% by 2035 from the 2013 levels, and by 73% by 2040.

But heavily polluting industries such as steel and cement production, oil refining and shipping are vital to Japan's economy. Fossil fuels generate a vast majority of its energy.

To bridge the gap, the government has said CCS is indispensable.

“It enables decarbonization in areas where transitioning to non-fossil fuel alternatives — such as electrification or the use of hydrogen — is challenging. Consequently, CCS has become indispensable for simultaneously achieving a stable energy supply, economic growth, and decarbonization,” a 2025 briefing by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said.

The ministry did not respond to an email from AP asking for comment.

Japanese companies have other CCS projects.

Off the coast of Chiba, where surfing made its Olympic debut during the Tokyo Games, a large platform juts from the water, marking where exploratory drilling is taking place for the Tokyo Metropolitan Area CCS project, a joint project between Inpex, Nippon Steel and others to capture CO2 from steel plants and store it offshore. Another Japanese company is also planning to ship emissions to Malaysia.

Environmentalists say the ramping up of CCS will prolong the use of heavily polluting fossil fuels.

“We see it as a greenwashing tactic that fossil fuel companies are using to green light continued pollution instead of doing the obvious choice of ramping down production and phasing out fossil fuels,” said Deng.

title: Nuclear Reactors for Merchant Shipping: A Total Cost of Ownership Assessment of a Low-Carbon Pathway
summary: The UCL Energy Institute's assessment of nuclear propulsion offers little immediate relief, confirming it is currently more expensive than conventional shipping. Economic viability hinges entirely on unproven reactor cost reductions and a robust IMO Net-Zero Framework, potentially making it competitive only after 2040. This stark reality underscores the industry's continued reliance on cheaper, high-carbon fuels, while "low-carbon pathways" remain distant and speculative.
content:
The report, Nuclear Reactors for Merchant Shipping: A Total Cost of Ownership Assessment of a Low-Carbon Pathway, was published by researchers from the UCL Energy Institute’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group, part of The Bartlett School of Environment, Energy and Resources.

The research found that without the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework (NZF), no nuclear-powered vessel is cheaper than a conventional ship, even at the lowest assumed reactor costs. With the NZF, nuclear propulsion could become the cheapest option from 2040, but only if reactor costs fall to levels not yet demonstrated.

Abstract

This study assesses the economic viability of nuclear-powered merchant shipping through a literature review, expert interviews and a total cost-of-ownership analysis.

The findings show that reactor costs and global greenhouse gas emissions policy are critical to the competitiveness of nuclear propulsion. Without the IMO Net-Zero Framework, no nuclear-powered vessel is cheaper than conventional ships currently in use, even at the lowest assumed reactor costs.

Under the NZF, nuclear propulsion could become the cheapest option from 2040, provided reactor costs fall significantly. However, these lower costs have not yet been demonstrated.

The research also identifies insurance, liability and regulatory frameworks as important barriers to adoption.

Published ahead of the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) meeting, scheduled for 30 November –3 December 2026, the report highlights the importance of effective global emissions policy in determining whether nuclear propulsion can become a competitive low-carbon option for shipping.

title: U.S. Targets Fraudulent Ship Registries Used by Iran’s Shadow Fleet
summary: The U.S. Treasury has exposed a fraudulent ship registry network, led by Suniel Kumar Sharma, enabling Iran's shadow fleet to evade international sanctions. This elaborate scheme impersonated legitimate flag administrations, providing false registrations and certifications for sanctioned tankers like the PING SHUN (IMO 9231901). Such unregulated vessels, operating outside proper oversight, likely contribute significantly to global maritime pollution through unchecked HFO usage and unreported emissions.
content:
The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a network of individuals and companies accused of operating fraudulent ship registries that helped Iran’s shadow fleet evade sanctions, while issuing a new warning to maritime companies about the risks of dealing with falsely flagged vessels.

The U.S. Treasury Department announced the sanctions on Wednesday as part of Operation Economic Outcast, targeting an India-based network led by Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid.

According to Treasury, the couple operated a network of fraudulent flag registries and maritime certification services that allowed sanctioned tankers carrying Iranian petroleum to continue operating under flags they were not legally authorized to fly.

Some of those vessels were transporting oil on behalf of Iran’s military and its proxies, Treasury said.

The network allegedly impersonated maritime authorities in countries including Guyana, Eswatini, Laos, Aruba, Nicaragua, and Sint Maarten, issuing registration documents and certifications without authorization from the governments involved.

In many cases, the operation relied on websites designed to look like legitimate national ship registries, offering everything from vessel registration to seafarer certification and classification services.

Treasury said the scheme dates back to at least 2014, when Sharma and Shahid sought to impersonate the flag administration of Dominica.

In 2023, Sharma established Singapore-based Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE Ltd., which continued providing registration services for vessels transporting Iranian oil even after authorities in Eswatini publicly disavowed the operation.

Among the vessels identified by Treasury was the sanctioned tanker PING SHUN (IMO 9231901), which had previously transported multiple shipments of Iranian oil.

The network also allegedly provided false flags to sanctioned tankers LATTAFA (IMO 9245794), BINARY STAR (IMO 9380570), and VERA (IMO 9304655).

Treasury cited the case of the MAJESTIC X, formerly PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was seized by U.S. military forces on April 22 while carrying Iranian oil. The tanker had been operating under a fraudulent Guyana flag.

The sanctions target Sharma, Shahid, two associates, and nine companies and organizations linked to the network, including Oceaniek Technologies India, Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited, and Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry.

OFAC Warns Maritime Industry Over False Flags

Alongside the designations, the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new industry alert warning that companies providing services to vessels operating under fraudulent flags could face sanctions or penalties.

The warning reflects a growing problem in the shadow fleet trade, where vessels increasingly rely on questionable or outright fraudulent registrations after being removed from legitimate flag registries.

OFAC said that while shadow fleet operators have long used frequent flag changes to obscure their activities, fraudulent registries have become an increasingly common way to keep sanctioned vessels operating.

These registries can create the appearance of legitimate registration even when the country whose flag is being used has never authorized the vessel to fly it.

OFAC urged insurers, financial institutions, and other maritime service providers to conduct additional due diligence when dealing with vessels showing signs of false registration.

Among the warning signs identified by OFAC are vessels with unknown flags, registration documents that cannot be verified, and discrepancies between a ship’s reported flag and the country code associated with its Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number.

The agency also warned about vessels claiming flags from countries without recognized ship registries.

The implications extend beyond sanctions compliance.

Flag states are responsible for overseeing vessel safety, certification, and compliance with international maritime regulations. Vessels operating under fraudulent registrations may lack legitimate regulatory oversight and valid insurance coverage.

Treasury warned that falsely flagged vessels could expose coastal nations to billions of dollars in potential environmental and economic damages in the event of a major maritime casualty.

OFAC also encouraged governments to investigate fraudulent registries operating in their names and report suspected cases to the International Maritime Organization so that maritime databases accurately reflect vessels with invalid registrations.

Broader Pressure on Iran

The measures are part of Operation Economic Outcast, a sanctions campaign launched in August aimed at cutting off the financial networks supporting Iran’s oil exports and other economic activities.

The latest action comes as the United States continues its maritime blockade of Iran amid the ongoing war, with Washington seeking to disrupt the networks that allow Iranian oil to reach international markets.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that companies and individuals continuing to support the Iranian government would face consequences.

“We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air,” Bessent said.

The sanctions package also included Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc., which Treasury said continued providing ground handling services to several sanctioned Iranian airlines.

The maritime designations and new OFAC advisory highlight Washington’s growing focus on the service providers and intermediaries that keep Iran’s shadow fleet operating, rather than the tankers themselves.

title: Efficiency and the new economics of shipping’s decarbonisation
summary: Shipping lines are finally acknowledging that basic operational efficiency, previously a mere cost-saving afterthought, now offers financial incentives by avoiding regulatory penalties. This shift is driven by the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, which directly monetise every tonne of CO2 emitted, forcing owners to re-evaluate their carbon intensity. While avoiding compliance costs for thousands of tonnes of CO2 is a minimal step, this belated focus on incremental efficiency must not overshadow the urgent need for drastic fuel transition.
content:
Oskar Levander from Kongsberg Maritime writes for Splash today.

For almost two decades, efficiency has been routine good practice in shipping. Owners have cut fuel burn and improved hull and propeller performance. These useful measures were often treated in isolation as cost control. However, this approach no longer fits the complexity facing the sector, nor the larger question of how to pay for decarbonisation. Efficiency can help fund it.

The EU ETS brought shipping into carbon pricing in 2024. It covers all intra-EU emissions and half of emissions on voyages in and out of EU ports. FuelEU Maritime penalises fuels that miss a GHG intensity target that tightens with each compliance period.

The IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework would apply similar logic to the global fleet: a worldwide fuel-intensity standard backed by emissions pricing. Ships that beat the target could earn tradeable credits; those that fall short would pay into an IMO fund. Member states are due to vote on adoption in December 2026. If adopted, rules could take effect from 2028.

These regulations give efficiency and clean energy sources a new value. It can earn money to fund new fuels and supporting technology.

For example, under EU ETS, every tonne of CO2 a vessel does not emit is an allowance the owner does not have to buy or surrender. As free allocation to shipping is phased out, a container ship saving several thousand tonnes of CO2 a year avoids a large compliance cost before any fuel savings are considered.

Many owners have yet to catch up. Payback calculations based on fuel savings alone now understate the return. Hull optimisation, wind assistance, propulsion upgrades, heat recovery and digital energy management each deliver lower fuel costs, avoided ETS allowances, lower FuelEU compliance costs, and, for fleets with verified data, premiums from charterers and green finance providers.

A recent Kongsberg Maritime study shows the change that is possible. The Kamsarmax design combines hull and propulsion optimisation, integrated energy management and wind assistance on long open-sea routes. Modelled against a conventional Kamsarmax on a similar trade, it cuts fuel use by more than 40%, and by over half on the most wind-favourable routes. Every tonne of fuel saved on European trades is a tonne less exposed to EU ETS, and it reduces the vessel’s overall FuelEU compliance costs. Additionally, the wind assistance technologies also earn the vessel a FuelEU reward factor.

Owners who still judge efficiency on fuel cost alone are underestimating the return. A project that looked like a seven-year payback in 2021 could instead be a three-year payback in 2026, before any premium from a greener charter rate or better finance terms is realised.

While carbon prices are volatile, banking on future compliance savings can be risky. The caution is fair, but EU carbon prices have risen as free allowances are withdrawn. Even at a modest price, the saving from lower fuel burn over a vessel’s two- or three-decade working life can outweigh the risk of a weaker carbon market. Waiting for price certainty means waiting for something that will never come.

Efficiency is also fuel agnostic. Whether ships run on methanol, ammonia, bio-LNG, hydrogen derivatives or a mix, a vessel that needs less energy will be cheaper to run. With rules still being written and the future remaining uncertain, that flexibility is worth a great deal.

Decarbonisation is as much a balance-sheet problem as an engineering one. Efficiency is the most practical lever owners have. Those who combine small gains, prove them with verified data, and put the savings back into the transition can fund their way through the next decade.

title: KR Releases 14th Issue of Decarbonization Magazine, Covering Marine Small Modular Reactors and First-Year FuelEU Maritime Compliance Trends
summary: The first year of FuelEU Maritime reveals a critical regulatory failure, as 92% of ships avoided penalties through compliance pooling. This widespread credit trading caused compliance surpluses to plummet 80% below the penalty level, proving the current framework offers no real incentive for actual carbon intensity reduction. While discussions on complex marine SMRs and methane slip abatement continue, immediate emissions accountability remains elusive.
content:
An examination of emerging regulatory frameworks for marine small modular reactors (SMRs), including challenges associated with their application onboard ships and safety approval.

An analysis of the first year of FuelEU Maritime, highlighting compliance trends and their implications for decarbonization strategies

Korean Register (KR) released the 14th issue of its quarterly KR Decarbonization Magazine on October 29. The latest issue covers emerging marine SMR regulation, the first-year results of FuelEU Maritime, and technologies to cut methane slip from LNG-fueled engines.

The issue opens with an examination of the regulatory frameworks for marine SMRs and the challenges of installing reactors on vessels, including safety assurance, maintenance requirements, and the cost and complexity of obtaining approvals. The article also reviews recent IMO revision work, the IMO–IAEA collaboration and KR’s own technical projects.

While the regulatory framework for marine SMRs is still under development, FuelEU Maritime, by contrast, is already in effect, and the magazine analyzes its first year of compliance. Ships that fail to meet the mandatory greenhouse gas intensity limits can avoid penalties by pooling their compliance balances with over-compliant vessels. According to KR’s analysis, approximately 92% of ships used pooling in the first year, while the price of compliance surpluses gradually declined to approximately 80% below the penalty level.

Turning from regulation to technology, the issue also features an interview with Minho Kang, Senior Vice President at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, on engine optimization and exhaust aftertreatment technologies. He discusses the company’s Methane Oxidation Catalyst System (MOCS), which oxidizes unburned methane escaping from LNG-fueled engines.

title: Hydrogen turbine tests mark progress in maritime decarbonisation project
summary: The EU-funded MARPOWER project reports prototype tests for a future fuel-flexible gas turbine, including 100% hydrogen combustion. While researchers test components, actual maritime carbon intensity remains unchanged, with existing fleets still heavily reliant on HFO. Such R&D offers distant hope, but does not address today's urgent FuelEU Maritime compliance or excessive emissions.
content:
An EU-funded project developing a fuel-flexible gas turbine system for ships has reported progress in hydrogen combustion, heat recovery and magnetic bearing technologies, as it reaches the halfway point of its four-year programme.

The MARPOWER project, coordinated by Finland’s LUT University, aims to develop an energy conversion system capable of operating on a range of alternative fuels, including hydrogen, ammonia, renewable methanol and renewable methane. The proposed system would provide onboard power generation and cogeneration, with improved thermal efficiency intended to reduce fuel consumption.

Two years into the project, researchers have completed the overall system design and developed detailed designs for its principal components. Several technologies have entered manufacturing and experimental testing, although integration and validation of the complete system remain to be undertaken.

Among the most significant advances is the successful testing of a combustion chamber prototype operating on 100% hydrogen. The prototype was manufactured and instrumented before undergoing testing in an atmospheric test rig, following computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and the installation of hydrogen supply infrastructure.

The results are informing the development of a second combustion chamber prototype, incorporating a more flexible air distribution system and further geometry optimisations. These modifications are intended to improve the system’s ability to accommodate different fuels with limited changes to the combustion equipment.

Improving efficiency through heat recovery

The project is also investigating ways to recover and reuse thermal energy within the gas turbine cycle and from its exhaust gases.

The group has manufactured and assembled a scaled prototype recuperator, designed to transfer heat within the turbine cycle. The unit, built at 1:100 of the proposed system’s capacity, has passed non-destructive testing and pressure testing at 22.3 bar.

The recuperator incorporates a new heat-transfer surface geometry and has been manufactured using automated robotic laser welding. Further experimental validation is planned.

Alongside this, the design of a complementary waste heat recovery system has been completed, covering the boiler, steam turbine, pump, generator and associated equipment. The combined approach is intended to improve overall energy efficiency and reduce fuel requirements.

The project also reports progress in the design of the system’s compressors and turbines. A new optimisation procedure for the high-pressure turbine’s internal cooling channels has produced a design requiring approximately 15% less coolant flow than estimates derived from standard literature correlations, according to simulations.

Magnetic bearings and digital modelling

MARPOWER’s high-speed rotating machinery requires bearing and control

technologies that can support the rotor while limiting mechanical wear.

Active magnetic bearings (AMBs) support the rotor without conventional

mechanical contact and allow its position to be actively controlled. As the group explains, this is an important part of the MARPOWER energy conversion system.

A new axial magnetic bearing has been manufactured and installed in an existing flywheel test rig, where initial impact and recovery tests have been completed successfully.

Researchers are also developing a scaled rotor and hydraulically actuated platform to investigate the behaviour of the proposed 2.7 MW rotor system under simulated ship movements, including surge, pitch and roll.

In parallel, a digital twin of the MARPOWER system is being developed to simulate the interaction of its components under different operating conditions.

An initial calibrated model has been established, with automated simulations covering part-load operation, variations from design conditions and fuel switching. Early sensitivity analysis has identified turbine inlet temperature, ambient temperature and compressor efficiency as important influences on power output and thermal efficiency.

The model will be progressively refined using experimental results as component testing continues.

Next steps towards shipboard integration

During the project’s remaining two years, attention will shift towards integrating the individual technologies and evaluating their performance under more representative operating conditions.

Two vessel case studies, involving a container ship and a cruise ship, will investigate engine-room arrangements and use digital simulations to assess energy consumption and emissions under different operating scenarios. The studies will also consider the potential for incorporating MARPOWER technologies into existing vessels.

Further work will address safety, regulatory compliance, lifecycle environmental impacts and costs.

Professor Jussi Sopanen, MARPOWER Project Coordinator at LUT University, said: “During the first half of MARPOWER, we have advanced the system design, developed key technologies and started generating experimental results. The challenge now is to bring these developments progressively together, extend testing under more representative conditions and generate the evidence needed to assess the complete system and its integration on board ships”.

The project involves 11 partners from six European countries, including Alfa Laval, the German Aerospace Center (DLR), the Technical University of Denmark and Chantiers de l’Atlantique. It is scheduled to continue until August 2028.

title: Alternative fuels need infrastructure: Why gas bunker vessels matter
summary: The industry's scramble to scale LNG bunkering infrastructure, as detailed by DNV, merely solidifies reliance on a fossil fuel with significant upstream and onboard methane emissions. While the LNG-fuelled fleet expands rapidly, creating demand, this 'transition' fuel still generates substantial CO2 and potent greenhouse gas equivalents. This continued focus on fossil gas infrastructure delays urgent, substantial investment in genuinely zero-emission fuels required to meet climate targets.
content:
As shipping’s fuel landscape becomes more diverse, attention is increasingly turning to the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale. DNV’s latest white paper explores the growing role of gas bunker vessels, technical matters to be aware of, and the challenges and opportunities associated with supporting LNG today while preparing for the fuels of tomorrow.

The maritime industry is entering a period of growing fuel diversity. While much of the discussion focuses on fuels, engines, and regulations, the transition will also depend on the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale. DNV’s new white paper, Gas bunker vessels – Facilitating the transition to alternative fuels, details how gas bunker vessels are becoming a critical part of that infrastructure and analyses the key factors shaping their future development, from market growth and vessel design to safety, operational readiness, and the adoption of emerging fuels such as ammonia.

LNG success creates a new supply challenge

LNG has become the most widely adopted gaseous marine fuel and the first to achieve large-scale commercial deployment. According to DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform, around 900 LNG-fuelled vessels are now in operation worldwide, excluding LNG carriers. Around 650 additional vessels are expected to join the fleet before 2030, further increasing demand for LNG as a marine fuel.

As the LNG-fuelled fleet expands, pressure is growing across the entire bunkering ecosystem. LNG consumption by LNG-fuelled vessels increased by more than 500% between 2020 and 2024, with a further 167% growth expected between 2025 and 2030. The white paper argues that bunkering infrastructure is not keeping pace with this rapid expansion, creating a widening gap between fuel demand and available bunkering capacity.

“The LNG bunkering market is well supplied today, but the picture could change significantly as the LNG-fuelled fleet continues to expand,” says Martin Cartwright, Global Business Director, Gas Carriers & FSRUs, DNV Maritime. “Our analysis suggests the global LNG bunker vessel fleet may need to more than double by 2030, with between 165 and 208 vessels potentially required worldwide. Meeting that demand will require coordinated investment across the entire bunkering value chain, not just in the vessels themselves.”

Gas bunker vessels emerge as a key link in the alternative fuel value chain

The report argues that gas bunker vessels should be viewed as more than fuel delivery assets. As shipping adopts a wider range of fuels, they are becoming a critical link between fuel producers, storage facilities, ports, and vessels, helping ensure alternative fuels can be supplied safely, reliably, and at scale.

While gas bunker vessels share many characteristics with conventional gas carriers, their role as fuel suppliers creates a distinct operating profile. Frequent ship-to-ship transfers, interactions with a wide variety of receiving vessels, and the need to operate safely in busy port environments place additional demands on vessel design, operational procedures, safety systems, and crew competence.

“As the maritime industry adopts new fuels and technologies, understanding the bunker vessels that support the transition is becoming just as important as understanding the fuels themselves,” says Robert Østraat Kjelstadli, Principal Engineer, DNV Maritime, and co-author of the white paper. “These vessels are a critical part of the infrastructure that connects fuel supply with vessel operations. Safe and reliable fuel delivery depends on dedicated vessel designs, robust procedures, and the ability to operate efficiently across a wide range of ports and vessel types.”

Converting existing LNG vessels can accelerate capacity growth

Meeting future demand does not necessarily depend on newbuild vessels alone. The white paper highlights the conversion of suitable small-scale LNG carriers into dedicated bunker vessels as a practical way to accelerate capacity growth and support developing bunkering markets.

“Many of these vessels already possess the containment, cargo-handling, monitoring, and safety systems required for liquefied gas operations,” says Yury Ilchenko, Principal Engineer and Gas Carrier Specialist at DNV. “However, successful conversion requires more than adding transfer equipment. Owners must consider factors such as vessel compatibility, ship-to-ship transfer arrangements, vapour and pressure management, manoeuvrability, emergency response, and operational readiness to ensure the vessel can safely perform its new role as a bunker vessel.”

Bunkering safety must scale with LNG demand

As gas bunkering becomes more frequent and geographically widespread, maintaining consistently high standards of safety and operational performance becomes increasingly important.

Unlike conventional marine fuels, gaseous fuels introduce additional considerations around cryogenic handling, vapour management, pressure control, transfer operations, and emergency response. The white paper highlights how safety, resilience, and competence must develop alongside infrastructure if the industry is to scale bunkering operations successfully.

“Gas bunkering is not simply a matter of moving fuel from one vessel to another,” says Ilchenko. “It requires robust procedures, clear responsibilities, resilient systems, and competent people. As operations become more frequent and take place in more locations around the world, maintaining that discipline becomes increasingly important.”

Safe gas bunkering depends on people, procedures, and technology

The report stresses that safe and reliable bunkering depends on translating technical and regulatory requirements into consistent day-to-day practices. Structured safety management systems, compatibility assessments, ship-to-ship transfer procedures, emergency response arrangements, and competence development all have an important role to play.

“Safe gas bunkering is built on a combination of technology, procedures, and people,” says Cartwright. “Operators that establish strong safety management systems, invest in competence development, and adopt a structured approach to risk management will be best positioned to scale operations safely and reliably as demand continues to grow.”

Operational readiness should be considered from the earliest stages of vessel design through to routine bunkering activities. The paper also highlights the value of common operating standards, clear allocation of responsibilities, and the use of industry guidance and checklists to support consistent performance across different ports, vessel types, and operating environments.

Today’s LNG bunkering investments could accelerate future fuel adoption

While the report focuses primarily on LNG, it also examines the growing role of other gaseous fuels, particularly ammonia. Recent regulatory developments and updated class requirements are helping make dedicated ammonia bunker vessels a practical possibility, while many of the operational principles developed through LNG bunkering remain directly relevant.

At the same time, the paper argues that today’s investments in LNG bunkering infrastructure have value beyond LNG alone. The vessels, transfer systems, operational experience, and safety frameworks being developed now can help support future fuel pathways, including biomethane, synthetic methane, and ammonia. While the future fuel mix remains uncertain, the need for safe, reliable, and scalable bunkering infrastructure is not.

title: Wärtsilä completes milestone marine sector project to reduce methane emissions on vessels
summary: Wärtsilä and Chevron completed engine conversions on three LNG carriers, transitioning Wärtsilä 50DF engines to Spark Gas operation, ostensibly to reduce methane slip. This modification reportedly reduces methane emissions to a mere 1.1% of fuel use on an IMO E2-cycle average, a belated acknowledgment of LNG's significant methane problem. Such incremental fixes, while technically sound, do little to address the global fleet's escalating carbon intensity, nor will they shield operators from future FuelEU Maritime fines driven by overall GHG emissions.
content:
Technology group Wärtsilä has successfully completed the conversion of one engine on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel (DF) to spark gas (SG) operation. This conversion aims to lower greenhouse gas emissions from the vessels by reducing methane slip, un-combusted methane that can escape into the atmosphere from LNG fuel. Following the successful conversion of these first three vessels, three additional vessel conversions are planned for execution later this year and next year, bringing the total number of converted vessels to six.

This project represents a technical collaboration within the marine sector focused on addressing methane emissions from LNG-fueled vessels. Wärtsilä’s 50DF to spark gas conversion project will modify the engines in service to operate as spark gas, using spark ignition versus diesel pilot fuel to initiate combustion. This enables a more optimised combustion process, thereby reducing the engine methane slip and improving efficiency.

“Advancing lower-emission shipping will require both technology innovation and industry collaboration. Through projects like this, we can gain valuable operational insights, evaluate solutions and contribute to the collective experience needed to help move the industry forward while continuing to provide safe and reliable transport of energy,” said Barbara Pickering, President of Chevron Shipping.

The Spark Gas Conversion for the Wärtsilä 50DF engine minimises methane emissions by introducing an electrically controlled pre-combustion chamber valve. This enables a more optimised combustion process. The estimated result is that, on an IMO weighted (E2-cycle) average, the conversion reduces methane emissions down to 1.1 percent of fuel use. The solution is available to vessels in the industry with existing Wärtsilä 50DF engines for diesel-electric propulsion, the majority of which are LNG carriers.

“This achievement highlights the importance of technology development and cross-industry collaboration in advancing lower-emissions solutions for shipping. By working collaboratively across the marine sector, initiatives such as this project contribute to broader efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions,” comments Roger Holm, President of Wärtsilä Marine & Executive Vice President at Wärtsilä Corporation.

title: Ardmore Shipping: Decarbonization through the details
summary: Ardmore Shipping reports a 14% CO2 reduction to 361,656 tonnes in 2025, attributing the drop to efficiency technologies and B30 biofuel blends used for FuelEU Maritime compliance. However, the company admits this decrease also stems from altered "trade patterns, waiting time, and fleet utilization," obscuring the true impact of their touted "long-term operating discipline." Such reactive compliance, rather than aggressive fossil fuel phase-out, exemplifies greenwashing over genuine decarbonization efforts.
content:
The regulatory requirements governing environmental performance continue to ratchet up, with the EU Emissions Trading System in place for large ships entering EU ports since January 2024, FuelEU Maritime in effect since January 2025 and the IMO’s Carbon Intensity Indicator tightening. At the same time, negotiations continue over the IMO’s Net Zero Framework. For us, however, efficiency is a long-term operating discipline, not a reaction to each new rule.

At year-end 2025, we had 26 product and chemical tankers in operation and our latest Sustainability Report identifies 13 diverse energy efficiency technologies in use on our vessels, from Mewis Ducts and propeller boss cap fins to variable speed drives and low-load boiler optimization, as well as DeepSea’s AI-enabled voyage optimization, and weather-routing services from WetterWelt, all of which combine to support more fuel-efficient operations across the fleet.

In 2025, we also purchased and used biofuel blends of up to B30 to achieve full FuelEU Maritime compliance. Our technical teams and onboard crews made that possible, managing fuel handling, storage and combustion while safeguarding vessel performance throughout the voyages. Their work showed that biofuels can be operationally viable at scale.

This progress is borne out in the data. Fleet emissions decreased from 422,083 metric tons of CO2 in 2024 to 361,656 in 2025, a 14% reduction. Trade patterns, waiting time in port, drydocking days and fleet utilization also influence year-on-year emissions, so the decrease cannot be attributed to any single measure. Our focus instead is on sustained improvements in vessel efficiency and fuel consumption.

In 2025, our fleet recorded zero Port State Control detentions, and 81% of Port State Control inspections recorded zero deficiencies. This, in turn, is only made possible by our people. Seafarers can access on-demand training through the AFLIX app, use virtual reality to familiarize themselves with vessels before joining, and provide anonymous peer feedback on safety competencies through our Safety Rating app. Every member of our shore-based team also visited a vessel during the year, strengthening the connection between ship and shore. What’s more, our WAVES initiative, which supports women at sea, helped grow our community of women officers from 16 to 25 in 2025.

As regulatory requirements evolve, we will keep improving vessel efficiency through practical investment, informed decision-making and the expertise of our people. Technology has an important role to play, but its value depends on how effectively it is integrated into day-to-day vessel operations. That commitment to continuous improvement is central to how we deliver performance and progress.

title: Alternative-Fuel Ship Orders Outpace Port Bunkering Infrastructure, Lloyd’s Register Warns
summary: Lloyd's Register reports a concerning disconnect: 1,942 alternative-fuel vessels are on order, yet port bunkering infrastructure remains critically underdeveloped. For example, only 25 ports offer methanol bunkering for 385 ordered methanol-capable ships, while ammonia bunkering is available at a single port for 45 ordered vessels. This infrastructure deficit implies many 'alternative-fuel' ships will continue burning conventional fuels, undermining genuine decarbonization efforts and risking higher operational carbon intensity.
content:
The global shipping industry is ordering alternative-fuel vessels faster than ports can develop the infrastructure needed to fuel them, according to a new report from Lloyd’s Register (LR), highlighting a growing challenge for shipowners investing in cleaner propulsion technologies.

LR’s new Fuel for Thought: Ports report, released Monday, found that 1,942 alternative-fuel-capable vessels were on order as of January 2026, representing 47% of the global orderbook by tonnage, according to Clarksons Research.

But the infrastructure needed to support those ships varies dramatically depending on the fuel.

Liquefied natural gas (LNG) bunkering was available at 222 ports worldwide, compared with just 25 ports actively offering methanol. Commercial ammonia bunkering, meanwhile, has been recorded at only one port, following the first operation at Ulsan, South Korea, in April 2026.

The disparity is particularly significant given that shipowners have ordered 385 methanol-capable vessels and 45 ammonia-capable ships, according to LR.

“The fleet is moving faster than the infrastructure needed to support it,” said Kamran Ul Haq, Senior Vice President of LR Ports Advisory. “An owner can order an alternative-fuel vessel today, but that does not mean the fuel will be available where that ship needs it. Fuel strategy and trading strategy can no longer be considered separately.”

The findings come amid a renewed surge in alternative-fuel vessel orders, led overwhelmingly by LNG.

As gCaptain reported in October, data from DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform showed that shipowners ordered 69 alternative-fuel vessels in September, the highest monthly total in nearly two years. LNG accounted for 48 of those orders, with new contracts spanning containerships, car carriers, bulk carriers and ro-ro vessels.

The surge brought alternative-fuel orders to 311 vessels through the first nine months of 2026, up 53% from the same period a year earlier.

LNG’s dominance reflects its relative maturity compared with emerging alternatives. With an established global supply network and commercially proven propulsion technology, LNG offers shipowners greater flexibility when deploying vessels across international trading routes.

Methanol, by comparison, is gaining ground at major bunkering hubs but remains limited in geographic reach. Ammonia is still at an earlier stage, with most ports pursuing the fuel focused on pilot projects, safety assessments and regulatory frameworks.

The challenge is particularly relevant for ports deciding where to invest.

Last week, gCaptain reported that the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach identified LNG and methanol as the most viable alternative marine fuels for the near and medium term.

Their joint Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment recommended a phased approach to infrastructure development, relying on existing ship-to-ship bunkering capabilities for LNG while pursuing methanol pilot projects and improvements to safety and permitting requirements.

The Southern California findings closely mirror LR’s conclusion that ports should focus on fuels with credible demand rather than attempt to accommodate every emerging technology.

“Ports do not need to back every fuel,” Ul Haq said. “They need to understand where credible demand will emerge and put the safety, regulation, skills and partnerships in place to respond.”

LR also found that alternative-fuel infrastructure remains concentrated in a relatively small number of shipping hubs, particularly Northern Europe, North Asia and Singapore. That concentration makes access to fuel along specific trade routes increasingly important when owners evaluate newbuildings and vessel conversions.

Biofuels offer a more immediate alternative because compatible blends can generally be supplied through existing bunker infrastructure. LR’s Fuel Oil Bunker Analysis and Advisory Service recorded drop-in biofuel deliveries at 90 ports over the previous 12 months, although the 13 leading ports accounted for 77.5% of recorded quantities. Singapore alone represented more than a quarter.

Hydrogen, meanwhile, remains largely confined to demonstration projects and short-sea applications.

The report also underscores the distinction between making alternative fuels available and ensuring they deliver meaningful emissions reductions.

As gCaptain recently examined, LNG’s rapid adoption has brought increased scrutiny of methane slip, the unburned methane released from ship engines, particularly as European emissions regulations place greater financial consequences on greenhouse gas performance.

The climate benefits of methanol and other emerging fuels likewise depend heavily on how they are produced, making the availability of genuinely low-carbon fuel supplies another challenge beyond bunkering infrastructure.

For ports, LR says the next phase of the transition will depend on targeted investment, regulatory readiness and closer coordination with shipping companies and fuel suppliers.

Berth-specific risk assessments, licensing, emergency response capabilities and workforce training will be essential to moving alternative fuels from trials into routine commercial operations.

“For ports, investment should follow credible demand rather than trying to prepare for every fuel at once,” Ul Haq said. “Named vessel programmes and green shipping corridors are also ways to reduce infrastructure risk, alongside early investment in safety frameworks, licensing, emergency preparedness and workforce skills.”

The central message for shipowners is that ordering a vessel capable of burning an alternative fuel is only part of the transition. Ensuring that fuel will be available, affordable and commercially viable along the ship’s intended trading routes is becoming just as important.

title: PortXchange says measuring emissions isn’t enough
summary: PortXchange highlights a critical industry failure: many ports treat emissions reporting as an end, not a starting point for genuine decarbonisation action. Their expanded EmissionInsider platform aims to bridge this gap, offering multimodal monitoring, forecasting, and AI-assisted planning to finally integrate emissions data into operational and investment decisions. This overdue integration is essential to hold ports accountable for their scope 3 emissions contribution from vessels, directly impacting carbon intensity and potential FuelEU Maritime fines for the maritime sector.
content:
Ports have spent years improving how they calculate and report emissions. But knowing how much a port emitted last year does little to guide tomorrow’s investment decisions.

That frustration has emerged repeatedly in PortXchange’s conversations with ports seeking better ways to manage their environmental impact. They want to understand emissions across their operations, anticipate future changes and assess the consequences of major investments.

PortXchange is responding by expanding EmissionInsider, with new features coming to the platform including multimodal emissions monitoring, emissions forecasting, scenario modelling and AI-assisted decarbonisation planning. Ports’ practical needs are shaping these developments, as they want to use emissions information to guide operational and investment decisions.

Sjoerd de Jager, Managing Director & Co-Founder of PortXchange, believes the industry has spent too long treating emissions reporting as the end of the process rather than the starting point. “Ports have become much better at measuring emissions, but measuring them doesn’t make them disappear,” de Jager said. “If the information sits in a report that nobody uses when making operational or investment decisions, we have to question what we’re achieving. Ports need to know where they can make a difference, what it will cost and whether their plans will actually reduce emissions.”

Eugene Sypachev, Head of Engineering at PortXchange, is leading the development programme and sees a need for closer cooperation between sustainability teams and those responsible for daily port operations.

“In most ports today, sustainability and operations run as separate conversations. One team owns the annual number, the other owns the daily throughput target, with little shared data connecting the two,” said Sypachev.

“We want to give people across the port a clearer picture of operational activity and its emissions consequences, so environmental performance can be considered when decisions are made rather than assessed afterwards.”

Looking beyond vessel emissions

Much of the maritime industry’s attention has focused on vessel emissions, but ships are only part of a port’s environmental footprint. Trucks, rail movements, and cargo-handling equipment also contribute, and many ports still struggle to understand their combined impact.

PortXchange is developing EmissionInsider’s multimodal capabilities to bring these sources together, giving ports a clearer view of which activities drive most emissions and where reductions are possible. The company is among a relatively small group of technology providers pursuing emissions monitoring across multiple transport modes.

The expanded platform is being organised around four connected products: Emission Report, Emission Dashboard, Emission Simulations and Emission Strategy.

The Emission Report will provide structured emissions reporting for ports with different levels of data availability. Emission Dashboard will support more regular monitoring of port activity and emissions, helping sustainability and operational teams follow changes in performance and measure progress against their targets.

Understanding what comes next

Many planned capabilities come directly from discussions with ports that want to understand how changes in traffic, operating conditions, and future investments could affect emissions.

The forecasting capabilities will help ports anticipate short-term emissions changes. For example, weather disruptions or changes in vessel schedules can increase waiting times at berth or anchorage and lead to additional emissions. Using vessel movement information and emissions calculations, the platform aims to give ports a clearer picture of the potential environmental impact of these changes.

For longer-term planning, Emission Simulations will allow ports to examine the likely effects of different decisions before committing resources. Scenarios could include introducing shore power, electrifying port equipment, changing vessel speed limits or preparing for higher traffic volumes.

De Jager added: “Ports are under pressure to spend millions on decarbonisation, but how many can confidently say which investments will make the biggest difference? We cannot keep asking ports to make expensive decisions based on assumptions. They need evidence before the money is spent.”

Different ports, different priorities

Emission Strategy will introduce AI-assisted support for ports developing or reviewing their decarbonisation plans. It is being designed to help sustainability teams consider relevant measures and establish priorities based on their port’s operations, emissions profile and objectives.

For some ports, the immediate priority is establishing a reliable emissions baseline. Others already have detailed reduction targets but need to understand how planned investments or operational changes could help them meet those commitments.

“Every port’s journey starts in the same place: reporting, driven by regulation or by community demand for transparency. What comes next is where ports diverge,” Sypachev explained.

“A smaller port with limited resources may need help establishing its first reliable emissions baseline. Another may already have a detailed decarbonisation plan but need better information about which investments will deliver results. We are developing EmissionInsider to support those different needs rather than expecting every port to follow the same path.”

title: Alternative fuels comprised 12% of NYK’s marine fuel mix in 2025
summary: NYK Line reports a mere 12.2% of its FY2025 marine fuel mix came from 'low GHG' sources, leaving a staggering 87.8% dependent on conventional fossil fuels. Despite an increase to 297,000 tonnes of biofuel, the claimed 200,000 tonnes CO2e reduction against HFO offers only a marginal impact on NYK's overall emissions profile. A B100 pilot project commencing in May 2026 on a single vessel highlights the glacial pace of genuine decarbonization, as the vast majority of NYK's fleet remains tied to high-carbon fuels.
content:
Low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions marine fuels accounted for 12.2% of Japanese shipping company NYK Line’s total fuel consumption in the financial year 2025 (FY2025).

Japanese shipping company Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK Line) continued to expand its dual-fuel fleet, operating 35 such vessels in the previous financial year, up from 26 in 2024. The figures exclude LNG carriers and LNG-ready vessels, the company said.

Biofuels comprised the largest share of NYK Line’s marine fuel mix during the mentioned period, followed by LNG.

Biofuel consumption rose to 297,000 mt in FY2025, continuing an upward trajectory from 251,000 mt a year earlier and a baseline of 6,000 mt in FY2023.

The shipping company is actively “increasing the use of biofuels and alternative fuels available today to achieve immediate GHG emissions reductions.”

NYK Line’s progressive shift toward low-emission marine fuels helped the company to reduce its emissions by 260,000 mt of CO2 equivalent (CO2e) in FY2025, it said.

Biofuel usage cut emissions by an estimated 200,000 mt CO2e relative to energy-equivalent heavy fuel oil like HSFO, NYK Line said, adding that the emissions reductions were verified by ISCC certification.

The shipping company laid a groundwork for broader biofuel adoption with the launch of a 12-month B100 (100% biofuel) pilot project aboard a car carrier in May 2026.

The biofuel is derived from used cooking oil. The trial focuses on monitoring engine durability following continuous use of B100 and developing safe operational guidelines.

title: MOL Holds Joint Naming Ceremony for World’s 1st 3 Ammonia-Fueled Capesize Bulk Carriers- New Beginning for Vessels Powered by Next-Generation Fuels as Group Moves toward Net-zero Emissions by 2050
summary: MOL held a naming ceremony for three ammonia-fueled Capesize bulk carriers (RURI MIRAI, RURI SEKAI, RURI HIKARI), yet these "world's first" vessels will not be operational until early 2027. Despite claims of "net-zero emissions," the announcement omits details on green ammonia sourcing, safety protocols for 3,000m3 tanks, or the significant NOx emissions from ammonia combustion. dirtiestships.com will rigorously scrutinize these 209,800-tonne ships' actual carbon intensity and FuelEU Maritime compliance post-delivery, beyond marketing rhetoric.
content:
Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd. announced that on October 29, MOL held a joint naming ceremony at CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding Co., Ltd., part of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), for the world’s first three ammonia-fueled Capesize bulk carriers, which are being jointly developed with the Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH NV (Note 1). Upon their scheduled delivery starting around early 2027, they will be jointly owned by MOL and CMB.TECH. MOL plans to operate the vessels under long-term charter contracts.

With CMB.TECH CEO Alexander Saverys and MOL Managing Executive Officer Kazuhiro Takahashi on hand for the ceremony, along with numerous stakeholders, the three vessels were respectively named the RURI MIRAI, RURI SEKAI, and RURI HIKARI.

As a co-owner and charterer of these vessels, MOL is working closely with internal and external stakeholders to formulate safe operating procedures and develop and establish comprehensive safety measures. These vessels will form MOL’s first net-zero-emission fleet.

Because ammonia does not emit CO2 during combustion, it is attracting attention as one of the next-generation fuels expected to support the decarbonization of the shipping industry. These vessels represent an important milestone toward achieving net-zero emissions.

Environmental strategy is a key element of the MOL Group’s management plan, “BLUE ACTION 2035.” In the “MOL Group Environmental Vision – BLUE ACTION 2035 Phase 2,” the group aims to begin operating net-zero-emission ocean-going vessels in the 2020s and achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. By providing safe, high-quality transport services using ammonia-fueled vessels, the MOL Group will promote the wider adoption of ammonia fuel and contribute to the realization of a sustainable society.
