title: Offshore Industry Sends Urgent Call To EU Policymakers For Fit-For-Purpose EU ETS And MRV Framework
summary: Offshore industry associations are petitioning the EU to delay their inclusion in the EU ETS from 2027, citing an "unfit" MRV framework that could "distort competition." This "urgent call" suspiciously aligns with an effort to circumvent upcoming carbon costs, despite their self-proclaimed role in Europe's energy transition. Robust, unambiguous emissions accounting is critical for all vessels; special exemptions or delays only enable continued high-carbon operations under the guise of "strategic assets."
content:
Eight maritime associations including the Royal Belgian Shipowners’ Association (KBRV) send an open letter to EU policymakers urging them to ensure a fit-for-purpose framework for the European offshore sector under the current EU ETS review.

The offshore shipping sector is a strategic asset to the European economy, playing a leading role in the continent’s energy transition, energy security and industrial competitiveness.

Yet the current EU ETS framework, entering into force beginning 2027 for offshore vessels, will distort competition and create opportunities for circumvention, based on a Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) framework that was not designed for offshore operations and is widely recognised as not fit for purpose.

The sector strongly urges EU policymakers to first ensure that a fit-for purpose activity-based MRV framework is operational, before the inclusion of offshore vessels above 5000GT in EU ETS from next year onwards.

Below is the open letter the sector has addressed to the European Parliament and members of the Council

EU ETS REVIEW: GET THE FRAMEWORK RIGHT FOR EUROPE’S OFFSHORE SECTOR

Open letter to Members of the European Parliament and EU Member States’ Permanent Representatives.

Europe’s offshore industry is a strategic asset. European companies are global leaders in the construction and maintenance of offshore windfarms, seabed, subsea infrastructure and other critical maritime infrastructure. Their vessels play an essential role in Europe’s energy transition, energy security and industrial competitiveness.

The undersigned associations fully support the EU’s climate objectives and the principle of carbon pricing. However, the planned inclusion of offshore vessels above 5000GT in the EU ETS from 2027 will impose significant financial obligations, distort competition and create opportunities for circumvention, based on an MRV reporting framework that was not designed for offshore operations and is widely recognised as not fit for purpose.

Our three calls to EU policymakers

1. Safeguard the international level playing field for offshore vessels. Identical offshore operations must face the same CO₂ costs, regardless of the port from which a vessel operates. The revised legislation should establish a clear activity-based system and close loopholes that will incentivise operators to mobilise vessels from non-EU ports.

2. Get the framework right. Define offshore activities, worksites and ports of call clearly, including seabed-related work. Replace unsuitable cargo, passenger and transport-work metrics and unnecessary voyage-by-voyage reporting with proportionate, harmonised, aggregated reporting.

3. Get the timing right. Do not impose ETS surrender obligations on offshore vessels until a revised, fit-for purpose MRV framework is implemented and demonstrated its ability to support reliable, fair and consistent emissions accounting. This is a sequencing request, not an exemption from carbon pricing!

Why this matters

Unlike conventional shipping, offshore vessels do not primarily transport cargo or passengers between ports. They perform specialised, project-based activities such as installation, construction, maintenance, dredging and inspection at offshore worksites. Applying traditional concepts such as cargo, transport work and voyage based reporting therefore does not reflect their operational reality.

More importantly, the current framework will distort the level playing field. Equivalent offshore activities can face different ETS exposure depending on the vessel’s deployment port: emissions will be fully covered when operating from an EU port, while the same activities from a non-EU port fall outside the EU ETS. This will shift offshore activity outside Europe, result in carbon leakage and weaken Europe’s strategic offshore capacity.

Offshore vessels of above 5000GT are nevertheless due to enter the EU ETS from 2027, before a fit-for purpose activity-based MRV framework is operational. Given the major flaws in the current methodology, this approach is disproportionate. The EU ETS and MRV review should therefore ensure that the reporting framework is fixed before ETS surrender obligations apply.

We urge the European Parliament and the Council to use the review to deliver one clear, fair and enforceable regime for offshore vessels.

title: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: Lower feedstock costs weigh on Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price
summary: Rotterdam's B30-VLSFO and B100 biofuel prices have significantly decreased, driven by cheaper feedstocks and Dutch ZRE A tickets. This widening discount, especially when factoring FuelEU Maritime compliance, positions these fuels as a more cost-effective alternative for regulatory adherence. However, the true carbon intensity reduction from these fuels remains dubious without robust, independent lifecycle emissions verification, challenging claims of genuine decarbonization.
content:
Europe

Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has dropped $36/mt in the past week, even as the Dutch port’s conventional VLSFO price has gained $23/mt over the same period.

This has narrowed Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $59/mt to $96/mt.

Prima Markets’ ARA UCOME and POMEME barge prices, both indicators of feedstock sourcing costs, have each dropped $57/mt in the past week, to $1,625/mt and $1,695/mt respectively. That leaves UCOME at a $70/mt discount to POMEME.

Lower feedstock costs most probably pressured Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price.

Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO (POMEME) is priced at $1,360/mt, an $87/mt discount to the port’s conventional LSMGO price.

B100 has been priced at $1,162/mt in Rotterdam today. Rotterdam’s B100 price has fallen by $188/mt over the past month, while its LSMGO price has risen by $77/mt. This has widened B100’s discount to LSMGO from $10/mt to $275/mt.

Pricing B100 for the same energy as a tonne of LSMGO, and including EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) costs and FuelEU Maritime compliance, B100’s discount to LSMGO has widened by $222/mt to $740/mt in the same period for a ship sailing from Rotterdam to another EU port.

The price discounts have increased demand for B100 in the Dutch port, a trader told ENGINE.

Dutch suppliers can generate ZRE A tickets for selling low-carbon fuels, and can trade the tickets with other suppliers. The price of these tickets has dropped from €240/mtCO2e ($269/mtCO2e) last Thursday to €235/mtCO2e ($262/mtCO2e) on Thursday this week.

These ZRE A tickets help lower Rotterdam’s biofuel prices compared with other ports. Belgium has no such mechanism.

In the neighbouring Belgian port of Antwerp, B100 (UCOME) has been priced at $1,973/mt today on an outright basis, down $1/mt on the week. That puts it at an $811/mt premium over Rotterdam’s outright B100 price before EU ETS and FuelEU costs are factored in.

In Portugal’s Aveiro, the B30-LSMGO price has dropped by $33/mt in the past week to $1,527/mt. Its B100 price has fallen by a steeper $92/mt to $1,553/mt.

Asia

Singapore’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has gained $63/mt in the past week to $1,191/mt, while the port’s conventional VLSFO price has risen $58/mt over the same period.

This has widened Singapore’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $5/mt to $189/mt.

Prima Markets’ price assessment for China UCOME cargo, which is a key feedstock for Singapore’s B30-VLSFO blend, has held at $1,220/mt, unchanged from last week.

Higher conventional VLSFO prices could have supported the blend’s price.

title: UK ETS site visits: key steps towards compliance
summary: UK ETS verification now mandates site visits, a crucial step to ensure shipping lines aren't just filing paper reports but genuinely account for their carbon output. However, the option for "virtual site visits" based on verifier "risk analysis" presents a potential loophole, raising concerns about thorough, on-the-ground scrutiny of actual vessel operations. These inspections are critical for validating Annual Emissions Reports, directly influencing carbon intensity calculations and potential penalties for operators failing to meet their obligations.
content:
UK ETS verification includes a site visit as part of the annual verification process. Maritime operators should prepare early on by ensuring their Emissions Monitoring Plan (EMP) is approved and by assembling the documentation needed to support verification of the Annual Emissions Report (AER). More about the UK ETS site visit requirements in this news.

Site visits under the UK ETS

Site visits are an important part of the annual verification of the AER. Without a site visit, the verifier is unable to verify the AER. The location and scope of the visit are determined by the verifier’s risk analysis and will focus on the management and monitoring of relevant emissions data. A site visit does not necessarily require attendance on every ship or at every location. DNV’s default approch is to visit the ISM Company.

An in-person site visit should normally be expected. A virtual site visit may be conducted only where the verifier concludes that it can provide reasonable assurance and the maritime operator obtains approval from the regulator. The operator’s application for a virtual site visit must include the information provided by the verifier, for instance on the outcome of the risk analysis, and be submitted by 28 February in the subsequent year. For example, where emissions are reported for the 2027 year, the application for a virtual site visit must be submitted no later than 28 February 2028.

Timeline and deadlines

The site visit is a prerequisite for finalizing verification of the AER. As the AER must be verified by 31 March 2027 for the first UK ETS reporting period (1 July to 31 December 2026), DNV recommends completing the site visit no later than the end of February 2027. A summary of the UK ETS timeline and deadlines:

For future reporting periods, DNV recommends aligning UK ETS site visits with other scheduled verification activities, such as EU MRV, FuelEU Maritime and relevant ISM company audits, where possible to reduce duplication and streamline preparations.

Prepare required documentation

Operators should prepare the documentation needed for the verification, including:

• The approved Emissions Monitoring Plan (EMP)

• The verifier’s risk analysis

• Data-flow activities and control procedures

• The applicable regulator’s approval for a virtual site visit

• A complete list of vessels covered by the maritime operator’s AER

• Verification report from the previous year (if verified by another verifier)*

The EMP is maintained at company level and describes the monitoring methodology, vessels under the operator’s responsibility and relevant emissions sources. Ship-level emissions are aggregated into one company-level AER, which must be verified before submission to the regulator.

Ship-level and company-level verification

Our current verification approach requires all ship-level emissions reports of the operator’s fleet to be verified by DNV. Supporting evidence documents, including applicable cargo samples, Bunker Delivery Notes (BDN) and Proofs of Sustainability (POS), should be provided through DNV’s OVD Admin in My Services on Veracity.

The company-level AER will be created in our My Services portal based on the maritime operator’s fleet. Verification can only be completed once the required site visit has been carried out, the EMP has been approved, and the vessel list and underlying ship-level information have been provided.

We are further developing our combined company-level and ship-level verification approach for the UK ETS. Further practical information on the process and required customer actions will be communicated as the approach is finalized.

title: Regular bioethanol bunkering begins at the Port of Santos
summary: CMA CGM has commenced regular bioethanol bunkering for its 13,000-TEU container ship, CMA CGM IRON, at the Port of Santos, promoting it as a decarbonization solution. While bioethanol *can* offer lower lifecycle emissions than heavy fuel oil (HFO), the actual carbon intensity reduction for this tri-fuel vessel, and the overall fleet, remains to be verified against CII targets. dirtiestships.com demands transparent data on the precise CO2 equivalent reductions per voyage and the continued reliance on fossil fuels in these "green" operations.
content:
[By Copersucar]

New phase follows the pioneering operation carried out in July, through a partnership between Copersucar, CMA CGM, Bunker One, AGEO Terminais, Santos Brasil and the Santos Port Authority, and reinforces Brazil's potential in the decarbonization of international shipping

Copersucar, a global leader in the sugar and bioethanol sector; CMA CGM, a global player in sea, land, air and logistics solutions; Bunker One, a subsidiary of the Danish Bunker Holding group, a global leader in bunker trading; and the Santos Port Authority (APS) announce the start of regular bioethanol bunkering operations for vessels at the Port of Santos.

The first operation took place this week, in October 19, with the bunkering of CMA CGM IRON, a 13,000-TEU container ship equipped with the world's first tri-fuel engine certified to operate on bioethanol: the Everllence-B&W G95ME-C10.5-LGIM.

The operation marks the transition from a pioneering experience to a regular bioethanol supply model, positioning the Port of Santos and Brazil as one of the leading low-carbon fuel bunkering hubs. By the end of this year, an additional multiple bunkering operations of CMA CGM vessels are planned with bioethanol supplied by Copersucar.

"Following the first operation carried out in July, we are now moving into a new phase, demonstrating that bioethanol can be incorporated into maritime operations safely, reliably and on a commercial scale. This initiative reinforces CMA CGM's commitment to accelerating the adoption of lower-carbon solutions and supporting the development of new energy ecosystems for the maritime sector", says Giovani Grassi, CEO of CMA CGM Brazil.

The bioethanol supplied by Copersucar comes from a consolidated and certified production chain. Sugarcane cultivation expands predominantly into degraded pastureland, while the RenovaBio program establishes strict sustainability and zero-deforestation criteria.

The market opportunity reinforces the potential of this initiative. Global demand for marine fuels exceeds 270 billion liters per year. Considering the energy equivalence between fuels, replacing just 10% of this consumption could represent an additional potential market of approximately 50 billion liters of bioethanol per year.

"This initiative marks a milestone for bioethanol and the maritime sector: it establishes the world's first green corridor for marine bioethanol bunkering and opens up a new global end market for the fuel. Through this initiative, Copersucar is enabling the use of bioethanol in regular commercial operations, connecting Brazil's production capacity and logistics infrastructure to international demand for decarbonization. This marks the beginning of a new growth frontier for the sector, with a renewable solution that already offers the availability, scale and competitiveness needed to advance in maritime transport", says Tomás Manzano, president of Copersucar.

The bunkering operations involve the coordinated efforts of several partners, connecting the stages of fuel production, transportation, storage and bunkering. Bioethanol produced by mills associated with Copersucar is supplied and transported to the Port of Santos by Evolua Etanol, a company that is part of the Copersucar ecosystem, where it is stored by AGEO Terminais. This logistics infrastructure enables the biofuel to be made available for ship bunkering.

At the bunkering stage, which takes place at the Santos Brasil terminal, Bunker One has developed a pioneering protocol for Latin America following months of studies and specialized team training, taking into account the fuel's low flash point.

For Antônio Carlos Sepúlveda, CEO of Santos Brasil, hosting this type of operation at Tecon Santos reinforces the company's commitment to the sustainable development of logistics in Brazil. "We have been working hard to reduce the carbon footprint of our operations and those of our customers. Contributing to the energy transition in the maritime sector is also part of this agenda," he says.

"Brazil has recognized the potential of bioethanol for decades. Now, we are bringing this experience to international shipping, combining Brazil's production capacity with Bunker One's expertise and global reach. By leading this initiative, the Port of Santos is positioning itself as a strategic destination for shipowners seeking to reduce their emissions, while other markets are still making progress on regulations for this type of bunkering," says Flavio Ribeiro, CEO of Bunker One LatAm.

According to Anderson Pomini, president of the Santos Port Authority (APS), "APS and all the partners involved in this operation have made history in global shipping and international maritime trade, a sector responsible for more than 90% of the world's trade transactions, by becoming pioneers in ship bunkering with bioethanol. This is a defining step toward a new era of sustainable development. We are very happy and proud to have achieved this milestone."

title: China charts course for green corridors
summary: China is positioning itself in "green shipping corridors," involved in 21 initiatives leveraging its green fuel production and battery technology. However, the commercial viability of these routes remains questionable, with customer demand identified as the weakest link. dirtiestships.com demands tangible carbon intensity reductions and verifiable emissions data from these projects, not just aspirational green fuel production targets.
content:
China is emerging as an influential player in the global green shipping corridor movement, leveraging its dominance in green fuel production, battery technology and maritime infrastructure to take a leading role in efforts to decarbonise international shipping.

Yet despite holding advantages across much of the value chain, the country still faces significant challenges if it is to convert ambition into commercially viable zero-emission trade routes.

A report from the Global Maritime Forum on China’s progress with green shipping corridors noted that China was involved in at least 21 green corridor initiatives as of June 2026, representing “nearly a fifth of the global green corridor portfolio”.

According to the report, China possesses strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks needed to successfully develop green shipping corridors: viable zero-emission fuel pathways, cross-value-chain collaboration and an enabling policy environment. Customer demand remains the weakest link.

“China holds strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks necessary to successfully realise green corridors,” the report said. It adds that the country is positioning itself “as a leading supplier of three zero-emission fuels and technologies central to the advancement of green corridors: methanol, ammonia, and electric batteries”.

That strength is built on China’s rapid expansion in green methanol and ammonia production, coupled with its emergence as a global leader in marine battery technology. The report highlights the country’s “low cost and early availability of green methanol and ammonia” and its position “at the forefront of marine battery development” as key competitive advantages. At the same time, China benefits from “innovative commercial partnerships and knowledge-sharing platforms across the value chain” and “rapidly strengthening policies related to green hydrogen”.

Green avenues

The report says that successfully developing green corridors could help China scale strategic hydrogen and battery industries, gain market share in a global bunker market worth approximately $100bn and participate in a wider maritime decarbonisation investment pipeline valued at between $1tn and $2tn. It could also support as many as four million green jobs while helping future-proof Chinese shipyards and maritime labour against the energy transition.

However, the report stresses that major barriers remain. For example, there are gaps in both “soft” and “hard” infrastructure, including fuel certification systems, bunkering networks and charging infrastructure. It also points to the risk of competition for green ammonia from domestic industries, difficulties maintaining alignment across corridor partnerships, high costs associated with alternative fuels and battery-electric vessels, and what it describes as “fragmented global demand for zero-emission shipping services”.

But the overarching challenge is economic.

While China may currently offer some of the lowest-cost green methanol and ammonia globally, those fuels remain significantly more expensive than conventional marine fuels. Likewise, battery-powered vessels still carry substantial capital cost premiums.

The report warns that customer demand has not developed at the same pace as supply-side initiatives. While some cargo owners are willing to pay higher freight rates for lower-carbon transport, willingness to absorb green fuel premiums remains inconsistent across markets. This creates uncertainty for project developers, shipowners and fuel producers attempting to make large-scale investments.

Against this backdrop, the report’s recommendations section focuses on a set of practical measures that could help move Chinese corridors from planning into operation.

Points for success

The first recommendation calls for accelerated development of infrastructure supporting methanol, ammonia and battery-electric shipping. The report argues that progress is needed in both certification frameworks and physical logistics networks. “This can be split into two focal points: soft infrastructure, aligning fuel projects with global certification standards, and hard infrastructure, the rollout of physical fuel transportation and bunkering networks,” the report noted. “Both are necessary to connect China’s green fuel production with the global shipping sector.”

Alignment with international standards is viewed as particularly important for routes linking China and Europe.

The report notes that compatibility with the EU’s Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin framework will be essential if shipping companies are to maximise regulatory compliance benefits under European legislation.

The second recommendation focuses on governance and collaboration. Drawing on lessons from green corridor projects around the world, the report says successful initiatives tend to share several traits, including clear governance structures, technology-focused targets, detailed feasibility studies and comprehensive implementation roadmaps.

The report also suggests that China can shorten development timelines by building on partnerships that already exist around fuel production, bunkering and offtake agreements. Rather than creating entirely new structures, corridor developers may be able to use existing commercial relationships as the foundation for broader decarbonisation projects.

A third recommendation centres on policy intervention to close the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels. “Both national and international policy action will be needed to support the success of green corridors,” the report says.

The authors argue that corridors connected to Europe already benefit from demand signals created by the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations. They also point to growing domestic support mechanisms in China, including green fuel incentives and hydrogen pilot programmes that could lower fuel costs and encourage early deployment.

Creating partnerships

Looking ahead, the report suggests there is scope for bilateral and plurilateral cooperation with major trading partners including the EU, Singapore, Australia and the United States. Mechanisms such as H2Global are highlighted as potential models for supporting green fuel deployment across international trade routes.

The final recommendation addresses what may prove the most difficult challenge: creating customer demand.

“Customer demand can be leveraged by targeting the shipping sectors that have demonstrated a higher willingness to pay and/or aggregating mechanisms,” the report argues.

The authors recommend focusing on first-mover industries with established climate commitments, particularly participants in the iron ore, vehicle and container sectors. Engaging cargo-owner alliances such as the Zero-Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance could also help consolidate demand and improve willingness to pay for green shipping services. Meanwhile, domestic policy measures aimed at reducing shipping carbon intensity among China’s state-owned enterprises may provide an additional source of early demand.

In its conclusion, the report presents a clear assessment of China’s position within the global maritime energy transition.

title: IMO launches Blue Solutions to support maritime decarbonization in Southeast Asia
summary: The IMO has launched "Blue Solutions," a multi-year project aiming to "assess and demonstrate" port and vessel decarbonization in six Southeast Asian nations. Funded by Germany with EUR 5.9 million until 2031, this initiative prioritizes studies on electrification and operational improvements, not immediate enforcement against high-carbon intensity vessels. While "capacity-building" and "knowledge-sharing" are admirable, the industry demands tangible reductions in HFO consumption and measurable improvements in carbon intensity, not prolonged discussions.
content:
IMO has launched Blue Solutions, a new project intended to support maritime decarbonization in Southeast Asia.

The announcement was made at the 51st ASEAN Maritime Transport Working Group (MTWG) Meeting in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

IMO will implement the project in collaboration with Partnerships in Environmental Management for the Seas of East Asia (PEMSEA) and six partner countries: Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Viet Nam.

A key feature of the project is its focus on ports, and their potential role in maritime decarbonization, helping countries assess and demonstrate solutions such as port and vessel electrification, cleaner technologies and operational improvements. The project will also support the development of greenhouse gas emission baselines and national action plans, and strengthen capacity-building, partnerships and knowledge-sharing across the region.

The project is funded by the International Climate Initiative (IKI) of the Government of Germany, with an initially approved budget of EUR 5.9 million for Phase 1, and is expected to run until January 2031.

The International Climate Initiative (IKI) said: “The transition to low-carbon shipping presents an important opportunity for Southeast Asia to strengthen its maritime competitiveness while contributing to global climate goals. Through Blue Solutions, we are pleased to support practical, country-driven action that can demonstrate scalable solutions and deliver tangible environmental and economic benefits across the region.”

Welcoming the initiative, Aimee Gonzales, Executive Director of PEMSEA highlighted the importance of linking ports with wider transport and coastal development strategies: “Ports are critical nodes connecting maritime transport, energy systems, industry and surrounding communities. By combining IMO’s expertise in maritime decarbonization with PEMSEA’s experience in integrated coastal management, including green port development, Blue Solutions provides an opportunity to support practical, locally driven solutions that deliver benefits both within ports and across the wider transport system.”

The project aims to support ports in moving from ambition to implementation, and to help create conditions for innovation, investment and the deployment of practical low-emission solutions across Southeast Asia.

Welcoming the launch of Blue Solutions, Jose Matheickal, Director of IMO’s Technical Cooperation and Implementation Division, said: “Maritime decarbonization requires strong partnerships. Through Blue Solutions, we are bringing together governments, ports, industry and development partners to identify practical solutions, build local capacity and create pathways for implementation. By working together, we can accelerate the transition to a more sustainable maritime future.”

title: Shipowners flag flawed EU emissions rules ahead of 2027 carbon tax
summary: A coalition of shipowners is lobbying the EU to revise emissions reporting rules for offshore vessels, claiming the current MRV system is ill-suited for their operations ahead of 2027 ETS inclusion. They seek an 'activity-based' system, warning that current rules could incentivize operators to mobilize vessels from non-EU ports, effectively seeking a different carbon cost framework. This "sequencing request" for revised MRV before ETS obligations, while not an exemption, appears a strategic maneuver to dilute imminent carbon pricing rather than drive genuine emissions reductions.
content:
The European Dredging Association (EUDA) and seven shipowner and offshore industry associations have called on European policymakers to revise emissions reporting rules before offshore vessels of 5,000 GT and above enter the controversial EU emissions trading system (EU ETS) in 2027.

The joint statement, addressed to the European Parliament and the Council, was also signed by KVNR, the Royal Belgian Shipowners' Association (KBRV), Armateurs de France, the Norwegian Shipowners' Association, Svensk Sjöfart, Danish Shipping and the International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA).

The associations said the monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) system was designed mainly for vessels transporting goods or people from one port to another.

Offshore vessels instead spend extended periods on installation, maintenance, dredging and inspection work at sea.

The group is seeking an activity-based system that would charge identical offshore operations the same CO2 costs, whatever port a vessel operates from. They warned that the current rules could encourage operators to mobilise vessels from non-EU ports.

The associations also want clear definitions for offshore work, work sites and ports of call, including seabed-related work. They are asking for reporting based on cargo, passenger and transport-work measures to be replaced by aggregated reporting.

They asked that ETS surrender obligations for offshore vessels begin only after a revised MRV framework has proved reliable. "This is a sequencing request, not an exemption from carbon pricing!" the statement said.

Offshore ships of 400 GT and above have been subject to MRV since January 1, 2025. Cargo and passenger ships of 5,000 GT and above entered the ETS in 2024. Port tugs were earlier exempted from the offshore-vessel monitoring requirements.

title: San Pedro Bay Ports Outline Path for Cleaner Marine Fuels: Methanol Bunker Demand Expected to Reach Up to 250,000 Tons By 2030
summary: The San Pedro Bay Ports laud their "Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment," projecting methanol bunker demand up to 250,000 tonnes by 2030. However, designating LNG as a "viable clean fuel" ignores its significant methane slip, while methanol's emissions are entirely contingent on its often fossil-fuel-derived production pathway. Without stringent well-to-wake lifecycle accounting, these initiatives risk merely shifting emissions, failing to genuinely reduce the fleet's carbon intensity or avoid future FuelEU Maritime penalties.
content:
The ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles have released a comprehensive report identifying promising clean marine fuels for oceangoing vessels and outlining steps to support their use at the nation’s busiest port complex.

Conducted as part of the ports joint Green Shipping Corridor efforts, the Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment examined which fuels are most likely to be adopted by the shipping industry calling at our ports, how much demand could develop locally and what infrastructure would be needed to support them.

The study found that liquefied natural gas (LNG) and methanol are the two most viable clean marine fuels for the near and medium term. Both offer potential pathways to reduce emissions from oceangoing vessels, depending on how the fuels are produced and sourced. Approximately 4,000 vessels call each year at San Pedro Bay ports. Reducing emissions from these vessels – the largest source of emissions in the ports complex – is a key to accomplishing Clean Air Action Plan goals.

“Strategic investments guided by this study will enable a growing market for these green marine fuels, helping ships serving the trans-Pacific transition to a cleaner future,” said Port of Long Beach CEO Dr. Noel Hacegaba. “The findings provide a promising path for us to work with our partners to continue improving air quality across the region in pursuit of our zero-emissions ambitions.”

”Reducing emissions from ships is one of the most important challenges facing our industry,” said Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka. “This study gives us a clearer picture of where the market is headed and how we can work with our partners to make cleaner marine fuels more accessible. It’s another important step in our ongoing commitment to cleaner air and a more sustainable supply chain.”

Among the study’s findings:

• Shipping lines are investing in a variety of fuel technologies, rather than moving toward a single alternative to conventional marine fuel.

• By 2030, annual demand at the two ports could reach approximately 65,000 to 115,000 metric tons of LNG and 64,000 to 250,000 metric tons of methanol, depending on market conditions and vessel deployment.

• Much of the storage and distribution infrastructure needed for early methanol fueling is already available or could be adapted, reducing the need for major initial investments.

• Fuel costs, shipping line commitments and regulatory requirements will help determine how quickly cleaner fuels become widely available.

The assessment recommends that the ports adopt a phased approach that includes incentivizing early methanol use, exploring pilot fueling projects, making use of existing storage facilities and working with regulatory agencies to establish clear safety and permitting requirements. For LNG, the study recommends focusing on existing ship-to-ship fueling methods to ensure safety and efficiency rather than constructing major new storage facilities at the ports.

The information contained in the assessment will help inform a joint ports Request for Proposal anticipated to be released by the end of the year that will solicit proposals to demonstrate alternative fuel bunkering capabilities in the San Pedro Bay.

The ports will also use the findings to help guide future planning and collaboration with shipping lines, fuel suppliers, terminal operators and government agencies as the maritime industry continues its transition toward lower-emission operations.

title: DNV outlines mandatory UK ETS site visit requirements ahead of 2027 deadline
summary: The UK ETS now mandates maritime emissions reporting from July 2026, requiring verified Annual Emissions Reports (AERs) and compulsory site visits by March 2027. DNV advises operators to complete site visits by February 2027, though the allowance for 'virtual visits' with regulatory approval warrants scrutiny for potential oversight gaps. Operators must furnish approved Emissions Monitoring Plans (EMPs) and comprehensive documentation, ensuring robust verification of actual carbon intensity, not just superficial compliance.
content:
The first UK ETS maritime reporting period covers July 1 to December 31, 2026, with Annual Emissions Reports (AERs) required to be verified by March 31, 2027. To avoid delays, DNV recommends completing site visits by the end of February 2027. The classification society has also advised the following:

Physical and virtual site visit requirements

Under the UK ETS, site visits are a mandatory part of the annual verification process. Their location and scope are determined by the verifier’s risk analysis, focusing on how emissions data is monitored, managed and reported.

A site visit does not necessarily require attendance on every vessel or at every company location. DNV’s standard approach is to conduct the visit at the International Safety Management (ISM) Company.

While physical visits are normally expected, virtual visits may be permitted where the verifier determines that they can provide reasonable assurance and the maritime operator obtains regulatory approval.

Applications for virtual visits must be submitted by February 28 of the year following the reporting period, accompanied by relevant information from the verifier, including the risk analysis findings. For the 2026 reporting period, this means February 28, 2027.

Documentation and verification requirements

DNV emphasizes that operators must have an approved Emissions Monitoring Plan (EMP), maintained at company level, identifying the monitoring methodology, vessels under the operator’s responsibility and relevant emissions sources.

Ship-level emissions data is consolidated into a single company-level AER, which must be verified before submission to the regulator.

To support verification, operators should prepare:

An approved Emissions Monitoring Plan (EMP).

The verifier’s risk analysis.

Documentation of data-flow activities and control procedures.

A complete list of vessels covered by the company-level AER.

Regulatory approval for a virtual site visit, where applicable.

The previous year’s verification report, where verification was conducted by another verifier, applicable from the second reporting period.

Early planning to avoid compliance delays

DNV recommends arranging site visits early and, where possible, coordinating them with existing EU MRV, FuelEU Maritime verification activities and relevant ISM company audits to reduce duplication and administrative burdens.

Operators are also encouraged to review their monitoring procedures, prepare supporting evidence and engage with their verifier ahead of the reporting deadline.

title: How big data is being used to reduce maritime emissions
summary: Shipping lines are leveraging "big data" from systems like Mitsubishi's MiPoLin to optimize ship design and operational efficiency. While presented as a decarbonization driver, this data primarily refines existing fossil fuel-dependent operations and future vessel concepts. Concrete, immediate reductions in carbon intensity for the current fleet, and avoidance of FuelEU Maritime penalties, remain largely unaddressed by these efficiency gains.
content:
Finding ways to reduce shipping’s almost 3% contribution to global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions — and help the sector achieve net zero by 2050 — is fueling industry innovation.

Already, alternative fuels like liquefied natural gas (LNG), methanol and ammonia are gaining traction, as they can be used in dual-fuel marine engines to help reduce overall GHG emissions. While air lubrication systems — which create a ‘magic carpet’ of bubbles to reduce friction, and therefore emissions, as a vessel carves through the water — have been deployed for some time.

Now the industry is using advanced data analysis in its drive to decarbonize as rapidly as possible. From optimizing routes for fuel reduction and predicting maintenance issues, to streamlining port operations and supply chains, data is enabling shipping companies to make the most efficient calls.

Another advantage of big data is that deeper analysis can reveal trends that might otherwise go undetected. Mitsubishi Shipbuilding, a part of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) Group, and National Maritime Research Institute, Japan (NMRI) have both accumulated extensive ship performance data through their activities. Their aim is to use these datasets to build and operate future ships more efficiently and cleanly.

To further enhance these efforts, the two organizations’ programs are working together. Mitsubishi Shipbuilding’s MiPoLin system leverages 100 years of ship performance data, including 1,200 tank test results and design data from more than 420 ships, to predict a vessel’s required power. It can also identify efficient hull forms for future ship designs and evaluate the performance of existing vessels.

NMRI’s programs — OCTARVIA-web for ship lifecycle fuel efficiency evaluation; SALVIA-OCT.-web for onboard monitoring data analysis; and EAGLE-OCT.-web for analyzing hull performance data — incorporate MiPoLin’s design data estimated from historical data into its own extensive onboard analysis, giving a fuller picture of the likely entire lifecycle performance of the ship in question.

All of these insights make it easier for shipping companies to choose more efficient hull designs up front, improve how ships are operated and, ultimately, reduce GHG emissions from the maritime sector.

title: Containership orderbook heads towards 16m teu
summary: The containership orderbook's surge towards 16 million TEU, representing 43.9% of the current fleet, guarantees a substantial increase in future absolute emissions. Maersk's order for twelve 24,000 TEU "LNG dual-fuel" megamax vessels, alongside other carriers, merely perpetuates reliance on fossil fuels with negligible emissions reduction and significant methane slip. With fleet capacity projected to expand by 9.2% in 2027 and 14.4% in 2028, the industry continues to prioritize volume over true carbon intensity reduction, inviting stricter FuelEU Maritime scrutiny.
content:
The containership industry’s extraordinary ordering spree is showing no signs of slowing, with the global orderbook now exceeding 15m teu and another wave of megamax contracts poised to push the total towards 16m teu before the end of the year.

The latest figures from Alphaliner show that approximately 40 additional large containerships are expected to join the newbuilding pipeline, involving Maersk, Yang Ming, CMA CGM and MSC.

Orders from the first two carriers are expected shortly, while contracts involving CMA CGM and MSC are believed to have been signed but have yet to be confirmed by Alphaliner.

Among the most significant prospective deals is Maersk’s return to the largest containership segment. Alphaliner reports that the Danish carrier is negotiating exclusively with Chinese shipyards for a series of twelve LNG dual-fuel vessels of 24,000 teu, potentially accompanied by options for another twelve. At an estimated $240m apiece, the initial programme would be worth approximately $2.88bn, rising to $5.76bn if all options were exercised. The ships would represent Maersk’s first entry into the 24,000 teu category, moving beyond the distinctive twin-engine Triple-E designs it introduced more than a decade ago. Chinese yards are being favoured on cost and available construction slots.

The orderbook’s expansion is particularly striking against the size of the existing fleet. Alphaliner’s October Monthly Monitor put contracted capacity at 15.12m teu, equivalent to 43.9% of the trading fleet. Its projections show fleet capacity expanding by 9.2% in 2027 and a further 14.4% in 2028. That supply wave is arriving just as the industry’s operating geography undergoes another fundamental change.

Sea-Intelligence reported this week that around 60% of deployed Asia-Europe capacity is now operating, or scheduled to operate, via Suez rather than around the Cape of Good Hope. Assuming security conditions permit, the consultancy expects further normalisation during the first quarter of 2027. Returning to shorter voyages will release effective vessel capacity into a market already facing accelerating physical deliveries.

Braemar warned in its latest container briefing that the combination of returning Suez services and the expanding orderbook was “not an ideal combination for charter rates”.

Jefferies has expressed similar caution over 2027, warning that newbuilding deliveries could push fleet growth ahead of cargo demand. Yet today’s charter market remains remarkably resilient.

Alphaliner reports that only 0.8% of the global cellular fleet was commercially idle in its latest survey, while charter rates have climbed to their highest levels in four years. Promptly available ships remain exceptionally scarce, with some large units reportedly commanding six-figure daily earnings.

The ordering boom is also reshaping propulsion choices. LNG dual-fuel ships now represent 56% of contracted capacity, compared with 12% for methanol dual-fuel vessels. Conventional propulsion accounts for just under 32%. Alphaliner recorded 2.3m teu of fresh LNG dual-fuel orders during 2026, with the anticipated megamax contracts potentially adding another 1m teu. Methanol ordering, by contrast, has almost stalled.

For now, geopolitical disruption and tight prompt vessel availability continue to underpin exceptional charter earnings. But Alphaliner cautioned that the coming delivery avalanche “will eventually take its toll on the market”.

title: Why the Shipping Industry Is Turning Its Attention to Nuclear Power
summary: Shipping's continued reliance on heavy fuel oil (HFO) generates approximately one billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent annually, alongside substantial SOx and NOx emissions, exacerbating air quality issues. While 46-72% of cruise ships *could* use shore power, only 3% of ports offer it, forcing berthed vessels to burn bunker fuel; now, the industry "considers" advanced nuclear for future solutions. This focus on distant nuclear technology conveniently sidesteps immediate responsibility for current carbon intensity, FuelEU Maritime non-compliance, and the urgent need to eliminate HFO usage today.
content:
Commercial shipping causes significant pollution, accounting for about 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, or roughly a billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent annually.

Heavy fuel oil combustion emits sulfur oxides (SOx), nitrogen oxides (NOx) and black carbon, worsening coastal air quality and causing respiratory illness.

Ships release millions of gallons of oily bilge water that spreads invasive species, along with fuel from accidental spills into marine habitats.

While between 46% and 72% of cruise ships utilize electric shore power, the technology is relatively rare; only 3% of ports offer Onshore Power Supply (OPS) services. The vast majority continue to allow berthed ships to generate onshore power using traditional diesel engines burning heavy bunker fuel.

This however, could be changing thanks to advanced nuclear technologies, which “are shifting from the theoretical into practical consideration for ports and the maritime sector,” states a new joint paper from the British Ports Association and Lloyd's Register.

"Advanced nuclear technology could reshape port environments, maritime operations and industrial energy systems. It offers potential benefits in reliable low-carbon power, shore power, industrial heat, fuel production, vessel propulsion, resilience and high-value maritime services.”

Potential applications include nuclear-powered ships, floating or transportable nuclear power units, and land-based small modular reactors (SMRs) or microreactors to power port operations and support fuel production, states World Nuclear News.

“Ports are becoming increasingly large electrical power consumers and some are exploring their own role in energy production,” the paper says. “Electrified cargo-handling equipment, cold storage, shore power, electric fleets, industrial tenants, data centres, hydrogen production and synthetic fuel pathways are all increasing demand for reliable, low-carbon electricity. Small nuclear reactors can provide stable baseload power for ports and reduce reliance on regional grids, depending on power demand, site location, regulations, grid constraints, and cost. Ports are often located at the intersection of constrained grids, heavy industrial demand, strategic logistics and local air-quality or decarbonisation pressures.

“Nuclear offers a possibility to provide for these new or increasing demands in a compact, reliable, low-emission package that is inherently safe.”

Out of only four civilian nuclear-powered merchant ships ever built, including the US NS Savannah and Russian icebreakers, the Russian cargo vessel Sevmorput is the sole commercial ship using nuclear propulsion.

Building a nuclear-powered container ship currently costs between $228 million and $582 million, compared to about $119.6 million for a conventional fuel-oil ship.

No small modular reactors (SMRs) are currently operating or actively powering port infrastructure, although the Port of Corpus Christi, Texas signed a Memorandum of Cooperation with the Maritime Administration (MARAD) in August 2026 to study SMR-powered port microgrids, shoreside power and floating nuclear energy systems.

The study by the British Ports Association and Lloyd’s Register suggests a single 100 Mwe-class SMR could in principle meet the electricity needs of a medium-sized port and several industrial tenants.

“The best candidates for port-based nuclear are likely to have large, steady and growing electricity demand, grid constraints, nearby energy-intensive industries, sufficient secure space, manageable site hazards, supportive regulatory or policy environments and strategic resilience needs. Detailed port-specific assessment is essential before any technology match or investment decision can be credible.”

Rather than rushing into nuclear, The paper proposes a tiered readiness model, enabling each port to adopt a proportionate level of ambition: from becoming 'nuclear-aware', with the ability to assess enquiries and engage authorities, through to 'nuclear-ready' and 'nuclear-enabled', or ultimately operating as a nuclear energy hub…

The paper concludes: "Advanced nuclear is not imminent for every port, nor is it a universal solution. But it is strategically significant and relevant to future energy demand such that port leaders should begin structured, proportionate planning in the near-term…

British Ports Association CEO Richard Ballantyne added: "For ports, the opportunities for advanced nuclear go beyond receiving a nuclear-powered ship. They are already planning for significant changes in energy demand, infrastructure and the vessels they serve. Advanced nuclear may not be the right solution for every port, but it is important that the sector understands the potential applications and starts asking the right questions early on."

The push to electrify maritime ports — replacing diesel-powered container-handling equipment such as gantry cranes, terminal tractors and reach-stackers with electric models — is creating a surge in localized energy demand. When combined with the high power requirements of shore power for docked vessels, ports are transforming into major electricity consumers.

This shift opens up a substantial opportunity for advanced nuclear technologies, specifically small modular reactors (SMRs) and microreactors to act as dedicated, port-side clean energy hubs.

Nuclear provides dependable 24/7 baseload power, making it well suited for high-density industrial applications where intermittent renewables like solar or wind fall short without large battery backups.
