title: Seven Japanese Companies Jointly Announce to Build and Operate Four Ammonia-Fueled Car Carriers and Commercialize the Ammonia Bunkering Business
summary: Seven Japanese companies jointly announced plans for four ammonia-fueled car carriers and a commercial ammonia bunkering supply chain in Japan's Chubu region, claiming a "world's first." While ammonia combustion is CO2-free, this "low-carbon ammonia" project lacks transparency on its lifecycle emissions, raising questions about its true climate benefit versus continued HFO reliance. dirtiestships.com will rigorously scrutinize these vessels' actual carbon intensity and FuelEU Maritime compliance, ensuring this isn't another costly greenwashing distraction from existing fleet emissions.
content:
Imabari Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. (“Imabari Shipbuilding”), Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, Ltd. (““K” LINE”), Kyokuyo Shipyard Corporation (“Kyokuyo Shipyard”), JERA Co., Inc. (“JERA”), Shin Kurushima Dockyard Co., Ltd. (“Shin Kurushima Dockyard”), Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (“NYK”), and Nihon Shipyard Co., Ltd. (“NSY”), jointly announced that they have agreed to develop an ammonia fuel supply chain in Japan’s Chubu region and to build and operate four ammonia-fueled car carriers supported by the supply chain.

Purpose and Overview of the Project

This project will be a comprehensive initiative to develop an integrated ammonia fuel supply chain, from the procurement of green ammonia and development of ship loading facilities to the construction of a dedicated bunkering vessel* with fuel supply through ship-to-ship (STS) bunkering,** and the operation of ammonia-fueled car carriers.

To address the need to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from international shipping as well as customers’ Scope 3 emissions, the seven companies aim to establish a stable ammonia fuel supply system through the integrated development of the supply chain. This project will be the world’s first commercial supply chain, with the Chubu region serving as the hub, integrating fuel procurement, supply infrastructure at the Hekinan terminal, and vessel operations.

Ammonia is a next generation fuel that emits no carbon dioxide (CO₂) when combusted and can be stored and transported in liquid form. In particular, steady progress is being made toward the practical use of low-carbon ammonia, which is produced with reduced CO₂ emissions during the manufacturing process, in the power generation sector. In the future, its use is also expected to expand into the transport sector, including maritime applications and other industries.

By combining their respective technologies, expertise, and infrastructure, the seven companies will establish an advanced integrated business model that brings together ammonia fuel procurement and supply, the construction of ammonia-fueled car carriers, and development of an ammonia bunkering vessel. Through this initiative, the companies will promote the decarbonization of international shipping through a Japanese industry collaboration while also supporting the broader utilization of ammonia for industrial and other applications. In doing so, they aim to contribute to the realization of a sustainable society and the development of a low-carbon ammonia market.

Fuel Procurement and Development of Ship Loading Facilities (JERA)

JERA is advancing the development of a lower-carbon ammonia value chain as part of its efforts to achieving net-zero CO₂ emissions from its domestic and overseas businesses by 2050, and contribute to global decarbonization and address the world’s energy issues. Its initiatives include the use of lower-carbon ammonia at the Hekinan Thermal Power Station for fuel substitution to decarbonize the thermal power generation business, and the installation of tank truck loading facilities to supply lower-carbon ammonia to other businesses.

Under this project, JERA will procure green ammonia produced using renewable energy. These supplies are intended to come from regions including India. In addition, JERA will develop new ship loading facilities at the ammonia receiving terminal adjacent to the Hekinan Thermal Power Station, which will establish a stable supply system for the bunkering vessel. JERA will contribute significantly to the decarbonization of international shipping and to Japan’s decarbonization efforts, with the Chubu region serving as a key hub.

Building of Ammonia Bunkering Vessel and Fuel Supply and Sales Structure (“K” LINE, Kyokuyo Shipyard, and NYK)

Kyokuyo Shipyard, which possesses advanced technical capabilities in building specialized vessels, will build the ammonia bunkering vessel. It is scheduled for completion in 2030, the same as ammonia-fueled car carriers. Following completion, the vessel will be owned and operated by NYK or a wholly owned NYK subsidiary.

“K” LINE and NYK will also establish a fuel sales joint venture, equally owned by the two companies, to facilitate fuel sales and supply between vessels. Using a bunkering vessel owned and operated by NYK or a wholly owned NYK subsidiary, the joint venture will supply ammonia fuel to car carriers through STS bunkering.

By combining the stringent safety standards and operational expertise the two companies have accumulated in handling ammonia and LNG, they aim to establish a safe, highly efficient fuel supply system.

Building and Operation of Four Ammonia-Fueled Car Carriers (Imabari Shipbuilding, “K” LINE, Shin Kurushima Dockyard, NYK, and NSY) “K” LINE and NYK are working to transition to next-generation fuels to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 and provide cleaner transportation services that meet society’s growing need for low-carbon and decarbonized solutions. Under this project, each company will introduce two ammonia-fueled car carriers, for a total of four vessels. Following their scheduled completion in 2030, the vessels are expected to transport finished vehicles for customers including Toyota Motor Corporation.

The vessels will be Japan’s first ammonia-fueled car carriers. They will be equipped with dual-fuel engines capable of using ammonia as fuel, as well as fuel tanks with sufficient capacity to enable trans-Pacific voyages using ammonia fuel alone.

To ensure the safe use of ammonia, which is toxic and corrosive, the vessels will also incorporate a multilayered safety concept, including measures to prevent and detect leaks and to neutralize ammonia in the event of a leak.

Drawing on the world’s most extensive track record in building car carriers, Shin Kurushima Dockyard will lead the basic design phase. The vessels will then be jointly designed and built by Shin Kurushima Dockyard, Imabari Shipbuilding, and NSY — each bringing deep, proven expertise in car-carrier construction.

title: European Shipowners reiterate key asks for EU ETS negotiations in Council and Parliament
summary: European shipowners are lobbying the EU to triple ETS revenues directed towards their "Sustainable Maritime Assistance Programme," effectively demanding public subsidies for their own decarbonisation. Despite representing 34.5% of global tonnage, their primary concern is "safeguarding competitiveness" by externalizing the costs of transitioning away from high-carbon fuels, rather than fully internalizing pollution expenses. This push for increased public funding, including for "all technologies," raises concerns about greenwashing and a delayed commitment to substantial investments in truly zero-emission solutions needed to meet stringent FuelEU Maritime goals.
content:
European shipping is a geopolitical asset for Europe, facilitating the export and import of goods, food and energy. While the EU represents around 15% of global GDP, the European fleet represents 34.5% of the world’s fleet in terms of global tonnage across all segments.

As the European Parliament and the Council advance their work on the Commission proposal for the EU ETS revision, European Shipowners | ECSA highlight the key amendments needed for the revision to deliver on shipping’s energy transition while safeguarding the competitiveness of European shipping.

A recent study found that shipping accounts for around 10% of EU ETS emissions but contributes almost 20% of ETS revenues. The new mechanism is an opportunity to reinvest part of this contribution in shipping’s energy transition. However, the 110 million allowances proposed by the Commission cover only a third of what is needed.

We call on the policymakers to:

• Reinvest ETS revenues in shipping’s decarbonisation. Shipping generates EUR 9 billion a year in national and EU ETS revenues. A recent study found that SMAP should be tripled from 110 million to 330 million allowances to help build a market for sustainable fuels and technologies.

• Support all technologies. SMAP’s scope should be extended and cover all technologies that deliver carbon savings, including energy efficiency projects.

• Make SMAP predictable. Predictability is essential: companies need certainty, before they take investment decisions, that the price gap between sustainable and conventional fuels and technologies will be partly covered. Companies should be able to apply for support for fuels and technologies in advance.

• Reward EU production. SMAP should incentivise the production of fuels and technologies in Europe through bonus points rather than made-in-Europe requirements.

• Earmark a dedicated envelope for shipping. The general earmarking of Member States’ ETS revenues should include a specific percentage or envelope for shipping.

• Apply one system to offshore vessels. The Commission has rightly recognised the need to change the rules applicable to offshore vessels, including the port call definition, to address unfair competition from non-EU offshore companies. However, applying one system from 2027 to 2030 and a different one from 2031 creates an unnecessary administrative burden.

Only the new rules should apply.

• Maintain, extend and improve derogations. Derogations for islands, outermost regions, ice-class vessels and transnational public services/obligations must be maintained, extended and made fit for purpose to support local economies, connectivity and regional cohesion.

• Support port competitiveness without distorting competition. ES|ECSA shares the objective of keeping EU ports competitive. To maintain a level playing field across all shipping segments, the transhipment exemption should be replaced by an annual Commission report on port competitiveness and infrastructure needs. Where needed, national ETS revenues should support port infrastructure upgrades.

• Simplify the EU MRV Regulation. Simplifying the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) Regulation is key to aligning the EU ETS, MRV and FuelEU Maritime, and to limiting the administrative burden on companies.

“Shipping pays almost 20% of total ETS revenues, although it accounts for only 10% of the emissions covered by the system, and, unlike other sectors, it has never received a single free allowance.

The European Parliament and the Council should at least triple the ETS revenues earmarked for SMAP to send a credible market signal for the scale-up of sustainable maritime fuels and technologies, including energy efficiency. Predictability is essential: companies need certainty, before they take investment decisions, that the price gap between sustainable and conventional fuels will be partly covered.

title: Maritime industry advances harmonisation of digital emissions reporting
summary: The Tripartite JIWG has released voluntary OVD and VER frameworks, aiming to standardise digital emissions reporting for better data exchange. These frameworks, however, create no new reporting obligations, offering administrative tidiness rather than mandating actual emissions reductions. dirtiestships.com demands concrete action on carbon intensity, HFO reduction, and FuelEU Maritime compliance, not just more efficient data mapping.
content:
The Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group (JIWG) has released two new frameworks that can help improve the exchange of operations and emissions data across the maritime industry.

The JIWG, chaired by BIMCO, was established under the Tripartite, a forum bringing together shipowners and operators, shipbuilders, and classification societies. As part of its work to develop a common approach for Maritime Emissions Reporting, the JIWG has released version 1.0 of the Operational Vessel Data (OVD) and Vessel Emissions Reporting (VER) frameworks. The two frameworks complement each other and can help establish a common foundation for a more efficient exchange of data.

Both OVD and VER are voluntary industry frameworks. They do not create new reporting obligations but provide a common approach that organisations may adopt to support more efficient and consistent data exchange.

The JIWG’s development of the OVD and VER frameworks complements and builds on earlier work by BIMCO and IACS (International Association of Classification Societies) to add emissions-reporting data elements to the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business. While the IMO Compendium provides common definitions and formats for maritime information, the latest work adds a practical implementation framework for exchanging operational vessel data and verified emissions-reporting results between industry systems.

The initiative also forms part of a broader move towards using the IMO Compendium as a common foundation for maritime data exchange. Emerging use cases covering port-call optimisation, electronic seafarer certificates and maritime emissions reporting demonstrate how common data definitions can support interoperability across different parts of the maritime sector.

The work of the group addresses the common industry challenge of stakeholders facing different reporting systems and data formats which often result in the same information being mapped, entered and checked multiple times.

The OVD and VER can support a more consistent, efficient and traceable exchange of data between ships, shipping companies, software providers, verification bodies and other authorised users. The approach will also make it easier to reuse data more consistently across the industry and connected value chains.

Two complementary parts of the data flow

The OVD provides a structured format for exchanging operational vessel and fuel-consumption data. It defines common data elements, names, units and structures, allowing the information to be interpreted consistently by different systems and organisations. It does not prescribe how data must be collected onboard, which software must be used or where data must be stored, but instead provides a common approach for sharing such data across the maritime industry.

The VER complements the OVD by providing standardised formats for emissions reporting in cases when commercial reporting practices and needs vary considerably. This could include charter-party performance, Emission Trading Schemes (ETS) cost allocation, FuelEU pooling and other commercial arrangements. The VER provides a common way to exchange emissions information, including its verification status for reporting periods that are defined by the user.

In practical terms, the OVD provides the underlying operational data layer while the VER provides a structured output solution for emissions information. In combination, the two solutions can help support the maritime industry’s objective of capturing data only once and reusing it for all relevant reporting, verification and other purposes.

See also the illustration in the annex, which shows the exchange of operational and emissions data across the maritime industry.

Responding to a growing reporting burden

The need for accurate and trusted maritime emissions reporting has increased due to the IMO Data Collection System (IMO DCS) and the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification system (EU MRV). Although these requirements serve different purposes, the use of different datasets and system formats can create inconsistencies, repeated data mapping and manual work across the reporting chain.

The Tripartite JIWG has therefore worked to develop a common approach that allows data to move between different systems, regardless of the technology or service provider used. The OVD builds on a framework initially developed by DNV and subsequently considered through the wider JIWG process. The VER builds on an initial draft prepared by ClassNK and was further developed collaboratively by the participating organisations.

Industry collaboration and practical implementation

As voluntary industry frameworks, OVD and VER version 1.0 provides a baseline for practical use and further development. Organisations can now consider how the formats may be applied within existing systems and processes. Experience from implementation and real-world use will help identify where definitions, guidance, tools or data structures may need further refinement.

As part of the next phase, the Tripartite Joint Industry Working Group will also assess options for transitioning OVD and VER towards independent and broadly representative governance. The objective is to establish clear ownership, open participation, transparent decision-making and predictable change management, providing confidence that the frameworks can be maintained as neutral and accessible industry resources.

The Joint Industry Working Group will continue to oversee the work while the governance alternatives are assessed and until an appropriate structure is ready to receive the frameworks. No final governance model has yet been selected.

Quotes

Yasuhiro Ikeda, Director, Digital Solutions Division, ClassNK

“VER is the result of a truly collaborative effort across all participating organisations, and I would like to thank everyone who contributed to this achievement. By establishing a common foundation for trusted and interoperable emissions data exchange, VER will help improve efficiency, transparency and digital collaboration across the maritime industry. Version 1.0 marks an important beginning, and we look forward to expanding its value through practical use and continued industry cooperation.”

Bjarte Walaker, Head of Maritime Deliveries, Veracity by DNV

“After several years of developing OVD, DNV is very pleased to see its broad adoption and grateful to the shipping companies, solution providers and other contributors who have helped turn it into a formal industry standard. This shared commitment is essential to enabling more efficient, consistent and interoperable exchange of vessel data, helping to reduce friction and support innovation across the maritime industry and connected value chains.”

Vincent Joly, Smartship Manager – Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore

“As reporting requirements continue to evolve, greater alignment in operational and emissions data is becoming increasingly important. Bureau Veritas has already adopted OVD for emissions data collection and supports this industry-led effort to establish common approaches for data exchange. These frameworks provide an important foundation for greater consistency across reporting and verification activities, enabling information to be shared and used more effectively across the maritime ecosystem.”

Michela Schenone, Marine Digital and Class Solutions Operations Director – RINA

“RINA believes that common industry standards are essential to make maritime emissions reporting more efficient, consistent and interoperable. RINA is taking practical steps to adopt OVD within its emissions reporting processes, supporting a common approach to data exchange across the industry. Continued industry collaboration will be key to achieving broad adoption and ensuring that these common frameworks deliver long-lasting value across the maritime sector.”

title: The EU is showing how regional maritime rules can support a global framework at the IMO
summary: The IMO's proposed Net-Zero Framework, already criticized as insufficient, failed adoption, leaving global shipping without a concrete carbon pricing mechanism. Despite the sector accounting for 3% of global emissions, oil-producing states and the US blocked progress, citing existing regional "burdens" like the EU ETS. This inaction ensures continued reliance on high-carbon fuels and delays meaningful decarbonization, highlighting the persistent failure to address shipping's substantial climate impact.
content:
In April 2025, governments at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) agreed on a historic global regulation, the Net-Zero Framework (NZF). It was designed to set global shipping on a course to net-zero by 2050 in a just and equitable way.

Global shipping is responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually, roughly as much as the economies of Germany or Japan.

If the current draft of the NZF were adopted, it would be a historic milestone in two key ways. Firstly, it would set common global targets for the world’s fleet to reduce carbon intensity of marine fuels. Secondly and more significantly, it could set the world’s first meaningful carbon pricing for a global industry. By collecting fees on any emissions that exceed agreed targets, it would raise $10-15 billion a year, providing financial support for clean fuels and for the sector’s transition in developing countries. Think investments in clean ports, zero-emission ships, and renewable energy production. If a ship reduces emissions enough to meet the targets, it would not have to pay at all.

While T&E analysis has previously shown that the NZF in itself is not strong enough to reduce shipping emissions at the pace countries agreed to, the agreement set an important global standard for a sector so far exempt from most climate rules.

The IMO’s failure to adopt the NZF as planned in October 2025 was a major upset not only for the industry, lacking the much-needed investment clarity and certainty, but also the world’s most vulnerable states who lack finance for their energy transition, while often facing the worst impacts from climate change.

One of the leading arguments put forward by the NZF opponents, largely oil-producing states led by the US and Saudi Arabia, was that there are regional carbon pricing measures already in place, and adding a global regulation on top would burden the shipping industry twice-over.

The EU’s carbon market, the EU ETS, which covers the EU’s share of shipping emissions on its trade routes, was identified by these countries as a barrier to agreement at IMO.

The IMO is expected to discuss adoption of the NZF again in December 2026. But while the blockers are still failing to propose any meaningful compromise, the EU has since proposed important changes to the EU ETS for shipping, addressing the concerns and paving the way for global and regional regulation to co-exist and reinforce each other.

There are three key signals sent out by the EU that should not go unnoticed by any government deciding on the future of the IMO NZF this year.

1. There will be no double pricing of emissions. The EU is clear that if the IMO establishes a carbon pricing scheme such as the NZF, a ship sailing internationally will not have to pay double for the same emissions under the EU ETS. T&E analysis shows that this overlap is already small, with only around 15% of relevant emissions covered by both ETS and NZF.

The NZF would become more strict over time, gradually increasing its coverage. As it does, the ETS would need to adjust – at least until 2040, after which global targets are yet to be agreed upon.

2. Alignment, not backsliding. Given that the NZF is insufficient to meet the IMO’s own climate targets, coordinated regional efforts are needed to fill the gaps. Currently, the EU reports emissions from all routes to and from its ports, but charges only 50% of the emissions. The newly proposed “ETS as a service” would allow EU trade partners to raise revenues on their own 50% shares through the EU’s existing system, without the administrative burden of setting up their own ETS from scratch.

3. The ETS should support an equitable transition. Whereas all funds would previously be spent only in European projects, around €100 million per year is now due to be set aside to fund shipping decarbonisation in SIDS and LDCs. In addition, countries linked through “ETS as a service” could also receive subsidies for green investments, further encouraging bilateral cooperation.

How would the two schemes interact in reality? Let’s take a ship in 2030, sailing from Tema, Ghana to Algeciras, Spain, emitting a total of 1080 tonnes of CO2 equivalent.

Under the EU ETS, the vessel would be charged for 41% of its emissions. The NZF, due to its limited pricing mechanisms, charges no more than 23%. Due to their different scopes, only 9% of the total is liable under both policies. This is the source of the alleged concerns, and the share of emissions that would now be exempted under the revised EU ETS.

Yet, to benefit from aligned rules, governments need to agree on a global deal first.

As the IMO meets for what many expect to be a decisive round of discussions this November and December, some countries are aiming to weaken or delay the agreement, in order to protect their oil interests. Despite their efforts and many proposals to reduce targets, create loopholes, or prioritise unsustainable options like LNG and crop biofuels, the NZF is still on the table.

Now, the EU is opening a path for its regional rules to co-exist with a global framework and involving others in the benefits. With the Commission having provided more clarity on how the ETS could co-exist with a global system, align with other regional measures and even provide some support to SIDS and LDCs, there is now even less justification for governments to use it as an excuse for weak action at a global level.

title: "Fit for 55": how the EU's new plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions will work
summary: The EU's "Fit for 55" package aims to tighten emissions caps and integrate maritime shipping into the Emissions Trading System (ETS) from 2023. This long-overdue inclusion acknowledges shipping's massive carbon footprint, with one vessel often emitting as much as 8,000 cars daily. While promising to increase the cost per tonne of CO2, the real test will be whether this translates into tangible reductions in carbon intensity and a shift away from high-sulphur HFO, or merely higher operational costs for polluters.
content:
The European Commission's new legislative package "Fit for 55" still needs to be approved by the EU member states and the European Parliament, but its main goals are already known and cover many key areas of the European Union's policy and economy.

This is stated in an article by Iryna Stavchuk, Deputy Minister of Environmental Protection and Natural Resources of Ukraine.

As is known, in July the European Commission published the "Fit for 55" legislative package aimed at revising the EU's current climate and energy targets for 2030. The package strengthens eight existing pieces of legislation and proposes five new initiatives across a range of policy areas and economic sectors: climate, energy and fuels, transport, buildings, land use and forestry, which will help achieve the set goal in the most effective way.

Revision of the EU Emissions Trading System

"Experience in recent years has shown that emissions trading is an effective and cost-efficient mechanism for reducing emissions, and the revenues it raises by auctioning emission allowances can be used by countries to support the transition to cleaner production and stimulate innovation," Stavchuk stressed.

As noted, the "Fit for 55" package includes a proposal to lower the overall emissions cap further and increase the annual rate of reduction by gradually cutting the number of CO2 emission allowances (including free ones) granted to companies under the EU ETS. This should lead to a higher price per tonne of emissions and thus encourage companies to reduce emissions. It is also proposed to phase out free emission allowances for steel companies and sectors covered by CBAM, as well as for airlines, while including maritime shipping in the system from 2023. The argument is that a single ship produces as much carbon emissions as 8,000 cars a day.

In addition, the EU intends to create a separate new emissions trading system for road transport and buildings heating and to start applying it from 2026.

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)

One of the new proposals in the document is the creation of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which will set a price on imports of a limited number of polluting goods based on the carbon emissions generated during their production.

"This measure is aimed at protecting European businesses from environmental dumping and preventing "carbon leakage" in situations where European companies want to relocate outside the EU to avoid paying for CO2 emissions. The mechanism is also intended to encourage industry outside the EU and to encourage the EU's international partners to take steps in the same direction," the Deputy Minister emphasised.

She noted that CBAM will operate in addition to the European Emissions Trading System, but instead of allowances, special CBAM certificates will be introduced, which importers will buy in the EU according to the volume of emissions generated in the production of their goods. Certificate prices will be calculated on the basis of the average auction price of EU ETS allowances. CBAM will initially apply to imports of fertilisers, electricity, cement and metallurgical products (iron, steel, aluminium) and will take into account only direct emissions from production. As noted, these are the sectors with the highest CO2 emissions and high trade intensity, which creates a risk of "carbon leakage" to other countries.

CBAM applies to companies from all non-EU countries, except those that participate in the European Emissions Trading System or have a national ETS linked to the EU one. This applies to members of the European Economic Area and Switzerland.

At the same time, it is noted that Ukraine can count on special conditions, namely an exemption from CBAM in the energy sector.

"The preamble of the document notes that as soon as third countries are closely integrated into the EU electricity market through market coupling, technical solutions should be found to ensure the application of CBAM to electricity exported from such countries into the customs territory of the Union. If no technical solutions can be found, third countries with market coupling should benefit from a temporary exemption from CBAM until 2030 at the latest, only for electricity exports, provided certain conditions are met. However, these third countries must develop a roadmap and commit to introducing a carbon pricing mechanism with a price equivalent to the EU ETS, and must commit to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, so as to align it with Union legislation on the environment, climate, competition and energy. This exemption should be withdrawn at any time if there are grounds to believe that the country concerned is not fulfilling its commitments or has not adopted an ETS equivalent to the EU ETS by 2030," Stavchuk said.

Changes in the transport sector

As noted, the EU wants to ban the registration of new petrol and hybrid cars in the EU from 2035. It also plans to tighten CO2 emission standards for cars and vans, which will accelerate the transition to zero-emission mobility. From 2030, average emissions of new cars must fall by 55%, and by 100% from 2035, compared to 2021 levels. As a result, all new cars registered as of 2035 will be zero-emission.

Under the revised Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, the EU plans to ensure the necessary roll-out of interoperable and user-friendly infrastructure for charging and refuelling clean vehicles across the entire EU, keeping pace with market developments and guaranteeing that rural and remote areas are covered too. This is because consumers are increasingly buying electric vehicles. That is why it is proposed to build charging stations for electric vehicles every 60 kilometres along the EU's main motorways, and hydrogen refuelling stations every 150 kilometres.

"In addition, the revised Regulation aims to put an end to the current lack of pricing transparency and to facilitate cross-border payments when charging electric vehicles. The European Commission has already announced its intention to increase the number of electric vehicle charging points to 1 million by 2025 and to 3 million by 2030," Stavchuk added.

Changes in the energy and renewables sector

As reported, energy production and use account for 75% of emissions in the EU, so accelerating the transition to a clean energy system is crucial for cutting emissions. The Renewable Energy Directive performs two main functions: it defines which energy sources are considered "renewable" and sets binding targets for renewable energy in Europe's energy mix. The revised Directive proposes a higher target of producing 40% of energy in the EU member states from renewable sources by 2030, compared to the previous 32%. The action plan states that all EU member states should contribute to this goal, and specific targets are proposed for the use of renewable energy in transport, heating and cooling of buildings, and industry. The sustainability criteria for the use of bioenergy are also to be tightened.

In addition, the European Commission has revised the Energy Efficiency Directive, which aimed to achieve savings of at least 32.5% by 2030. At present this target is not binding, but the European Commission now plans to make it a legal obligation. During the latest revision of the Directive, the European Commission also set more ambitious annual targets for reducing energy consumption at EU level. The Directive will set out how national contributions are determined and will raise the annual obligation to reduce primary energy consumption for member states from the current 32.5% to 39%. The public sector will have to renovate 3% of its buildings every year to drive the renovation wave, create jobs and reduce energy consumption and costs for taxpayers.

Also, the new version of the Energy Taxation Directive in the "Fit for 55" package proposes to align the taxation of energy products with EU energy and climate policy, promoting clean technologies and removing outdated exemptions and reduced rates that currently encourage the use of fossil fuels.

"The new rules aim to reduce the harmful effects of energy tax competition and will help secure revenues for member states from green taxes, which are less detrimental to growth than taxes on labour," Stavchuk commented.

Aviation and maritime fuels

The ReFuelEU Aviation initiative aims to reduce carbon emissions from fuel by increasing the amount of green jet fuel used in the EU. To boost the supply of sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs), the EU intends to introduce a fuel blending mandate. All aircraft departing from EU airports will have to refuel with green aviation fuel, with a minimum share of 2% in 2025 and 5% in 2030.

"Similarly, the FuelEU Maritime initiative will stimulate the uptake of sustainable maritime fuels and zero-emission technologies by setting targets for reducing the carbon intensity of fuels used by ships calling at European ports. Over time, these limits will become increasingly strict," the official explained.

Social Climate Fund and effort sharing between member states

As noted, the European Commission plans to set up a Social Climate Fund, which will provide member states with funding of EUR 72.2 billion for the period 2025-2032, based on a targeted amendment to the multiannual financial framework. In total, the Fund will mobilise EUR 144.4 billion for a socially fair transition by 2032. The Fund will be financed from the EU budget, and from 2026 it will also receive 25% of the revenues from allowance trading for companies that will pay for emissions from heating buildings with fossil fuels and from road transport under the newly created emissions trading system for road transport and buildings heating.

The European Commission has also revised the Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR), which covers agriculture, transport, buildings, waste and other sectors not covered by the ETS – in total, the ESR covers about 60% of emissions in the EU. The revised Regulation sets stronger emission reduction targets for each EU member state for buildings, road and domestic maritime transport, agriculture, waste and small industries. Recognising the different starting points and capacities of each member state, these targets are based on their GDP per capita, with adjustments to take cost-efficiency into account. However, the revised ESR should ensure a 40% reduction in emissions from these sectors by 2030 compared to 2005.

As the Deputy Minister noted, the "Fit for 55" plan needs to be approved by all EU member states and the European Parliament. At the same time, it is expected that the discussions on its approval may take at least one year.

Ukraine's climate commitments

As is known, Ukraine is also an active participant in the international fight against global warming.

"In 2016, the country was one of the first to ratify the Paris Agreement. In 2020, Ukraine joined the European Green Deal at a high political level, which aims to achieve climate neutrality of the European continent by 2050. In March 2021, the Government approved the National Economic Strategy until 2030, which forecasts quite significant industrial development and GDP growth. Moreover, according to this strategy, Ukraine is expected to achieve climate neutrality no later than 2060," Stavchuk emphasised.

"The draft Updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC2) – Ukraine's climate target for 2030 – is currently at the final stage of adoption by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine. In NDC2, Ukraine has set itself a more ambitious target of reducing GHG emissions to 35% of the 1990 level by 2030," the official summed up.

EcoPolitic previously reported that the EU had published a plan to combat climate change until 2050.

title: EmissionLink calls for EU ETS revenues to fund maritime carbon capture trials and port infrastructure
summary: EmissionLink proposes diverting EU ETS revenues to fund speculative onboard carbon capture trials and port infrastructure, risking subsidies for unproven technology rather than immediate decarbonisation. This "commercial viability" push for capture systems appears designed to avoid drastic cuts in current carbon intensity and continued excessive HFO usage. Instead of financing future hypotheticals, focus must remain on penalizing ships exceeding their CII ratings and ensuring FuelEU Maritime fines drive actual emissions cuts now.
content:
Maritime emissions specialist,EmissionLink, has called for a dedicated proportion of EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) revenues to be invested in onboard carbon capture trials and supporting port infrastructure, warning that the technology risks remaining commercially unviable without targeted financial support.

Philippos Ioulianou, Managing Director of EmissionLink, believes Europe has an opportunity to accelerate the development of maritime carbon capture by directing emissions trading revenues towards full-scale demonstrations that establish whether the technology can deliver verified emissions reductions at an economically sustainable cost.

The call comes as the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) moves to develop interim safety guidelines for onboard carbon capture systems. While welcoming the initiative, Mr Ioulianou argues that regulatory progress must be matched by investment in the infrastructure, emissions accounting mechanisms and commercial arrangements necessary to make the technology attractive to shipowners.

“Developing safety guidelines is an important step, but regulation alone will not persuade shipowners to invest in carbon capture,” said Mr Ioulianou. “Owners need a credible business case, backed by verified emissions savings, workable carbon disposal arrangements and a clear understanding of the financial benefits.

“Europe is well positioned to lead this work. Allocating a proportion of EU ETS revenues to onboard trials and port reception infrastructure would help establish whether carbon capture can become a commercially viable decarbonisation solution for shipping.”

EmissionLink is advocating investment in demonstration projects that assess every stage of the carbon capture process, from onboard collection and storage to offloading, transportation and permanent storage or approved use. Such projects should operate against clearly defined performance criteria and generate independently verifiable emissions data that can inform regulatory development and future investment decisions. However, EmissionLink cautions that onboard carbon capture is unlikely to be a practical solution for every vessel.

Ships operating on fixed and predictable routes offer the most promising early applications, as operators can plan carbon storage capacity and establish offloading arrangements at designated ports. For vessels trading on irregular routes or spot charters, the logistical challenges are considerably greater, particularly where carbon reception facilities and onward transportation arrangements are unavailable.

Technical suitability will also depend on factors including vessel age, available space, additional power demand and remaining commercial life. Ship owners and charterers must also resolve contractual questions surrounding additional fuel consumption, offloading delays and the allocation of regulatory compliance benefits.

“Installing carbon capture equipment introduces responsibilities that extend well beyond the initial investment,” Mr Ioulianou explained. “Shipowners must consider the operational impact, the demands placed on crews and who ultimately bears the additional costs. These questions need answering before the technology can be adopted with confidence.”

A further concern is the need for greater clarity around emissions accounting and regulatory recognition. While the EU ETS recognises qualifying carbon capture and permanent geological storage or chemical binding, practical monitoring, reporting and verification arrangements for maritime carbon capture remain underdeveloped.

Mr Ioulianou also warned that shipowners should not assume carbon capture benefits recognised under the EU ETS will automatically provide equivalent compliance advantages under FuelEU Maritime, which regulates the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used onboard ships rather than absolute emissions.

“Capturing carbon is not necessarily the same as delivering a verified reduction in emissions,” he said. “Shipowners need certainty over how those savings will be measured, independently verified and recognised under the relevant regulations. Without that clarity, it becomes extremely difficult to justify the capital and operating expenditure.”

title: EU Proposed SMAP subsidy favors e-fuels and bioLNG
summary: The EU's proposed Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) subsidy earmarks 110 million ETS allowances by 2040, primarily benefiting expensive e-fuels and bioLNG. This scheme offers up to 90% price gap coverage for e-ammonia and e-methanol, while conspicuously excluding widely adopted biofuels from used cooking oil and animal fats. Such selective intervention prioritizes future high-cost solutions, doing little to immediately curb the carbon intensity of today's dirtiest ships.
content:
Europe’s carbon market could soon start paying shipowners to switch fuels, but the support on offer is far from equal. In July, the European Commission proposed a revision of the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) that would reserve up to 110 million allowances between 2028 and 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, which is meant to cover part of the price gap between fossil marine fuels and sustainable alternatives. Rystad Energy’s analysis shows that, combined with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would reshape the cost ranking of marine fuels in Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels stand to gain the most, while biodiesel made from used cooking oil (UCO) and animal fats – one of today’s most widely used marine biofuels – is left out.

The timing matters. From 2026, shipping companies surrender ETS allowances for 100% of their verified emissions in scope, now including methane and nitrous oxide, while FuelEU Maritime requires a steadily tightening cut in the greenhouse-gas intensity of energy used on board. Both regimes rest on the sustainability rules of the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III). For shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers, the question is which fuel pathway the combined rules reward.

SMAP would cover 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with 10 additional percentage points where the feedstock is sourced in the EU. Because support scales with the size of the gap, the most expensive fuels receive the most per tonne, and EU-made e-ammonia could see its entire remaining premium covered (Figure 1). Support is halved on voyages into or out of the EU, and fuels generally must be produced in the EU or in a country with a linked carbon market.

Stacked together, the three instruments push several alternative fuels below the cost of very low sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO) on intra-EU voyages. At 3Q26 prices, bioLNG costs more than twice as much as VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at about half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are counted. Most of that advantage comes from FuelEU Maritime, and bioLNG would already undercut VLSFO without SMAP. Because bioLNG is a drop-in fuel for liquefied natural gas (LNG) engines, this strengthens the business case for LNG dual-fuel ships trading in Europe. RFNBOs receive the most generous treatment of all and, on paper, EU-produced e-ammonia could become the cheapest fuel on intra-EU routes, although very few ships can burn ammonia today and EU production remains small.

The clearest losers are liquid biofuels made from waste oils and fats. UCO and category 1 and 2 animal fats meet every EU sustainability test and earn full credit under both the ETS and FuelEU Maritime, but SMAP supports only advanced biofuels made from feedstocks listed in Annex IX Part A of RED III. Biogas, by contrast, appears eligible regardless of feedstock. The exclusion matters because of how Europe’s biodiesel industry is built. By 2030, crops and waste lipids such as UCO and other waste fats and oils are expected to account for about 96% of the region’s biodiesel and renewable diesel production capacity, leaving only around 2% clearly eligible for support (Figure 2). Aviation’s sustainable fuel mandate is drawing on the same waste lipids, meaning shipping is unlikely to secure much eligible liquid biofuel.

title: Maersk Tankers' Ammonia Power Tanker Retrofit Project Gets EU Funding
summary: Maersk Tankers secured EU funding for its "Ripple" project, proposing to retrofit four VLACs for ammonia dual-fuel engines. The company claims this initiative will avoid a mere 1.2 metric tonnes of CO2e over ten years, a figure so negligible it immediately raises greenwashing flags for such large vessels. dirtiestships.com will rigorously monitor these retrofitted carriers' actual carbon intensity and FuelEU Maritime compliance, demanding concrete emissions reductions beyond aspirational funding announcements.
content:
Maersk Tankers’ proposal to retrofit its Very Large Ammonia Carriers (VLACs) for ammonia power has been selected for funding by the EU Innovation Fund. The first-of-its-kind project, designed to adapt the large vessels to use ammonia as a marine fuel, is in keeping with the pioneering adoption steps by the industry for ammonia power.

The proposal submitted to the EU fund calls for retrofitting the ocean-going ships. Known as Ripple, the project envisions equipping the vessels with dual-fuel ammonia two-stroke engines as the first retrofit of its kind in the EU for a VLAC. Maersk Tankers reports the project will demonstrate the commercial viability of ammonia-fueled operations.

The company proposed retrofitting four of its VLACs, saying that by running on the fuel, the retrofitted carriers would avoid over 1.2 metric tonnes of CO2e in 10 years.

The EU Innovation Fund selected the Ripple Project as part of 77 additional projects designated for funding. The latest round for the fund was launched in December 2025, and according to the European Commission, it will entail €3.4 billion for investments. They noted it would reinvest the revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System into innovative decarbonization technologies.

The selected projects will begin negotiations to finalize their funding grants, including confirming budgets and timetables. The EU expects to complete the process in the first quarter of 2027 after the projects prepare grant agreements.

Maersk Tankers has taken delivery of the first two of a series of 10 VLACs it ordered. The first vessel, Jane Maersk, with a 93,000 cbm capacity, was delivered by HD Hyundai Samho in July. The vessel measures 221 meters (725 feet) in length. The ship is equipped to transport either liquefied ammonia or LPG. The second vessel, Jessie Maersk, was delivered to the company on October 21. The deliveries will continue until September 2028.

Samho highlights that because liquefied ammonia has a higher specific gravity than LPG, it requires advanced hull and unloading systems compared to conventional LPG carriers. The yard sees it as an emerging segment, noting it already has a backlog of 22 vessels worth $2.55 billion, including nine orders for VLACs it received this year.

title: World's 1st hydrogen engine for large ships cuts C02 emissions by 95%
summary: Japan Engine Corp. unveiled a hydrogen engine claiming a 95% CO2 reduction, yet Mitsui O.S.K. Lines' onboard demonstration is not slated until April 2028. This nearly five-year delay offers no immediate solution for current carbon intensity or impending FuelEU Maritime obligations. While hydrogen faces high costs and ammonia presents toxicity challenges, the industry's reliance on excessive HFO consumption remains largely unaddressed by such distant promises.
content:
The engine by Japan Engine Corp. was unveiled in early September and will be installed on a multipurpose ship to be built by Onomichi Dockyard Co., with Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd. expected to begin onboard demonstration testing in April 2028.

The engine adopts a high-pressure direct injection system to enable stable hydrogen combustion and implements safety measures such as double-walled piping for hydrogen supply lines, as the chemical element is prone to leakage and highly flammable.

In August last year, Japan Engine, based in Akashi in western Japan's Hyogo Prefecture, also completed what it called the world's first complete commercial ammonia-fueled engine.

While hopes are high for both hydrogen and ammonia to become next-generation fuels for large commercial vessels, challenges remain as the former faces the hurdles of high cost and slow adoption, and the latter requires stringent safety measures since it is toxic.

The International Maritime Organization has set a target of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and the Japanese government is supporting such efforts.

title: fuel fleet top $200B with over 1,350 ships
summary: More than 500 dual-fuel container ships and vehicle carriers are now operating worldwide and another 849 are on order, bringing total investments to over US$200 billion, according to the latest World ...
content:
More than 500 dual-fuel container ships and vehicle carriers are now operating worldwide and another 849 are on order, bringing total investments to over US$200 billion, according to the latest World Shipping Council data

The shipping industry needs to be able to source more commercially competitive alternative fuels to power these vessels

The WSC reiterated its call for the urgent need to have a global decarbonization framework to support future investment decisions

More than 500 dual-fuel container ships and vehicle carriers are now operating worldwide and another 849 are on order, bringing total investments to over US$200 billion, according to the latest World Shipping Council (WSC) data on it Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard.

As of September 2026, there were 503 dual-fuel ships on the water, up 41% from 358 in the same month last year. Another 849 ships are on order, bringing the total delivered or on order to 1,352 ships.

These ships are designed to operate on either conventional marine fuels or alternative fuel types, including renewable and lower-emission fuels, helping prepare the fleet for the transition to cleaner shipping.

“The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” WSC president and CEO Joe Kramek said in a statement.

“The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions,” he added.

READ: 3 PH firms seek fund, partners for sustainable aviation fuel projects

Global decarbonization rules needed ASAP

The latest figures show that alternative-fuel-capable ships remain the dominant choice for container ship and vehicle carrier orders. By deadweight tonnage, they account for 65% of container ship orders and 97% of vehicle carrier orders, compared with 23% across the rest of the global shipping fleet.

However, as the overall orderbook has expanded, orders for conventional-fuelled ships have also increased compared with a year ago. This comes amid continued uncertainty over global greenhouse gas regulation at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), highlighting the importance of clear global rules to support future investment decisions.

READ: Shipping emissions pact fails to get approval, talks to resume next year

“Ships ordered today will be operating for decades. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Kramek said.

WSC reiterated its strong support to a global greenhouse gas measure through the IMO, in line with its 2023 GHG Strategy.

It said a global measure is essential to closing the cost gap between conventional and renewable and near-zero emission fuels, while providing clear, consistent rules for international shipping. Without a global framework, shipping also risks facing a growing patchwork of regional emissions regulations, adding complexity and cost to global trade.

“We need a global measure with clear rules and strong, consistent enforcement that gives companies the confidence to invest in the production of cleaner fuels and the infrastructure needed to supply them,” Kramek said. “We trust IMO member states can come together to deliver that framework. Every delay means increased uncertainty, making the transition harder and costlier for the global economy.”

title: Shipping community issues clear call for IMO regulation to turn first-mover action into a global transition
summary: Global leaders from across the maritime value chain met in Shanghai this week for the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, where much of the discussion centred around the future of shipping’s ene...
content:
Global leaders from across the maritime value chain met in Shanghai this week for the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, where much of the discussion centred around the future of shipping’s energy transition.

With the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework facing a pivotal point in December, the Summit provided a timely opportunity for decision-makers to engage in crucial conversations about the industry’s green transition. By the end of the two days, a clear message emerged that IMO regulation will be essential to accelerating that transition, with many participants voicing support.

Among those present at the Summit was IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez, who spoke about the importance of a global regulatory framework in incentivising the investments the industry needs to reach the IMO’s net-zero targets.

“The goal remains in place: the decarbonisation of the sector is by 2050. We still need countries to invest in infrastructure beyond the IMO, and the energy sector to invest in new fuels. The more we diversify, the more resilient we are,” he said.

Over the last few days, shipowners, charterers, financiers, policymakers, and cargo owners had a rare chance to speak candidly, test assumptions, and understand each other’s priorities. Conversation topics ranged from decarbonisation and energy security to maritime governance and freedom of navigation, seafarer safety, and supply chain disruption.

“The value of a gathering like this is greatest when the stakes are highest, and the shipping industry is currently facing its fair share of challenges,” said Johannah Christensen, CEO of the Global Maritime Forum. “Leaders are facing fundamental dilemmas, like how to continue trading vital goods during times of rupture without risking lives. The Annual Summit 2026 provided an invaluable opportunity for them to come together with peers and discuss a path forward.”

New report reveals China’s strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks

This year’s Annual Summit, the first to be hosted in mainland China, provided an opportunity not only to connect with key Chinese business leaders and policymakers but also to learn more about China’s progress in the green transition.

Launched here in Shanghai, the Global Maritime Forum’s newest report looks at China’s strategic advantages in the four key building blocks considered crucial to successfully starting up a green corridor.

‘Green shipping corridors: How China is re-energising the global movement’ finds that China is one of the strongest actors globally in this space, holding strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks.

Swire Shipping CEO Jeremy Sutton announced as new All Aboard Alliance co-chair

Also at the Summit, the All Aboard Alliance announced Swire Shipping CEO Jeremy Sutton as its new co-chair, alongside existing co-chair and Circle Digital Ventures CEO Meei Wong.

“On behalf of Swire Shipping, it is an honour to be appointed co-chair of the All Aboard Alliance. Creating a safer, more inclusive, and respectful maritime industry is not only the right thing to do, it is essential to the future of shipping,” said Jeremy Sutton, Swire Shipping CEO and new Alliance co-chair. “I look forward to working with Alliance members to build on existing momentum and help create a vibrant maritime sector where everyone has the opportunity to succeed and thrive.”

The All Aboard Alliance’s work to develop global standards across ten areas of life at sea was a focal point across many discussions at the Summit. Participants agreed that the project is essential to the industry’s long-term future, particularly given the current context regarding seafarer safety in the Strait of Hormuz.

Annual Summit 2027 to be held in Copenhagen

In the closing session yesterday, it was announced that the Annual Summit 2027 will be held from 28-29 September in Copenhagen, Denmark.

Next year will mark the tenth anniversary of the Global Maritime Forum, which is headquartered in Copenhagen. Denmark’s long maritime history and integral role in the sector makes Copenhagen a natural place to host the tenth Annual Summit.

The Annual Summit 2026 was co-hosted by Shanghai Maritime University, with support provided by Summit partners Shanghai International Port Group, the People’s Government of Hongkou District, and Baltic Exchange.

“It has been our privilege to host key stakeholders from across the maritime value chain here in Shanghai. This year’s summit serves as a wonderful international exchange opportunity on the latest global shipping practices. We recognise the importance of stabilising market expectations and encouraging collaborative innovation. Shanghai Maritime University will endeavour to foster new forces for shipping development through talent cultivation,” said Professor Beiping Chu, President of Shanghai Maritime University.

“As a partner of the Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit 2026, Shanghai International Port Group congratulates the Forum on a successful gathering in Shanghai—a city and port that have long been a gateway for global trade—and the energy and ideas shared here give us confidence that, even amid uncertainty, our industry can work together toward a more resilient and sustainable future,” said Song Xiaodong, President of Shanghai International Port Group.

“We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the Global Maritime Forum and all partners. Let us work together to weather the storm, jointly advance the building of a maritime community with a shared future, and shape a greener, more inclusive and sustainable future for global shipping,” said Jie Cao, Deputy Director, Shipping Department of the People’s Government of Hongkou.

title: Copersucar signs first commercial deal to supply ethanol to ships
summary: Copersucar signed the world’s first commercial contract to supply ethanol to ships Thursday (22), together with fuel trader Bunker One and French shipping company CMA CGM. The agreement covers seven b...
content:
Copersucar signed the world’s first commercial contract to supply ethanol to ships Thursday (22), together with fuel trader Bunker One and French shipping company CMA CGM. The agreement covers seven bunkering operations by the end of the year, involving an estimated 10 million liters of anhydrous ethanol.

The number of bunkering operations may change depending on vessel availability and routes. Each operation will involve supplying part of a vessel’s fuel tanks, rather than filling the entire vessel.

The companies did not disclose the contract value, but Copersucar CEO Tomás Manzano said ethanol can be delivered to ships at a competitive cost compared with fossil fuels, or bunker fuel, when accounting for the cost a shipowner would incur to offset emissions by purchasing carbon credits—or the carbon credits it could sell by reducing its emissions.

The use of ethanol in ships has attracted growing interest from the maritime industry over the past year amid regulatory pressure to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from shipping, which accounts for around 2% to 3% of global emissions.

Although several alternative fuels are already available, Manzano argues that ethanol is the option that best meets the twin requirements of immediate availability and low carbon intensity. According to the executive, the ethanol supplied by Copersucar has a carbon footprint 75% lower than that of very low sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO), a fossil-based bunker fuel.

At current prices, anhydrous ethanol delivered to a vessel at the Port of Santos costs $300 to $400 per tonne more than VLSFO on an equivalent energy basis. However, because fossil fuel generates more emissions, the cost of abatement—the expense of purchasing carbon credits to offset emissions—ranges from $100 to $130 per tonne of carbon. “At this abatement cost, ethanol is on par with fossil fuel,” he said. The calculation assumes that replacing one tonne of bunker fuel with ethanol reduces emissions by three tonnes of carbon.

The agreement with Bunker One and CMA CGM was reached three months after an initial trial operation at the Port of Santos, when the three companies loaded a vessel with ethanol to assess operational safety. According to Giovani Grassi, CEO of CMA CGM Brazil, the test showed that “ethanol can be safely and reliably integrated into maritime operations on a commercial scale.”

The first of the seven bunkering operations covered by the contract took place last Monday (19), on a container ship with a capacity of 13,000 TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent units).

The fuel will be supplied to tri-fuel vessels, which can run on VLSFO, methanol, and ethanol. An estimated 70 to 100 such vessels are currently in service worldwide, with another 300 on order for delivery by 2030.

In addition to newbuilds, retrofitting methanol-powered dual-fuel vessels—and even conventional ships—is becoming increasingly viable. In the former case, modifications are simpler and involve only software and fuel injectors. But vessels powered by bunker fuel can also be adapted.

“Ships have very long service lives. If a shipowner can retrofit a conventional vessel during a scheduled dry-docking for maintenance, which must take place every five years, it can extend the vessel’s service life without having to build a new ship. At a much lower cost, the owner can switch to a solution that is already available,” said Flavio Ribeiro, CEO of Bunker One LatAm.

“A ship is a capital-intensive asset with a long service life. For an operator, flexibility is key to using whichever fuel is most competitive at a given time in terms of cost and carbon intensity,” Manzano added.

All bunkering operations under the contract will take place at the Port of Santos, in coordination with Santos Brasil, which operates the Tecon Santos container terminal, and AGEO Terminais, which operates ethanol storage tanks. To deliver ethanol to the ships, Bunker One adapted a barge previously used to transport bunker fuel so that it can now carry ethanol.

Manzano said Copersucar expects the agreement to establish a steady supply of ethanol to the maritime transport sector, with a target of 200 million liters for this purpose as early as 2027. To meet that goal, Bunker One is adapting another barge to handle larger volumes of ethanol between the Tecon terminal and vessels.

One of Copersucar’s goals for 2027 is to supply ethanol to ships in other countries, including Singapore. “The Port of Singapore handles more cargo in a month than Brazil does in a year,” Ribeiro noted. Another target is to supply ethanol to ships in the United States, where Copersucar markets domestically produced ethanol and has 12 terminals connected to ports.

title: EU’s Proposed Shipping Subsidies Could Make BioLNG Cheaper Than Fuel Oil
summary: The EU proposes a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, allocating 110 million ETS allowances to subsidize specific alternative fuels like BioLNG and e-fuels. This selective support aims to close the price gap with fossil fuels, yet notably excludes established biofuels like UCO-derived biodiesel, raising questions about market distortion. While purporting to accelerate decarbonization, this scheme risks greenwashing by picking winners and diverting focus from immediate carbon intensity reductions and persistent HFO consumption.
content:
Europe’s carbon market could soon start paying shipowners to switch fuels, but the support on offer is far from equal. In July, the European Commission proposed a revision of the European Union’s Emissions Trading System that would reserve up to 110 million allowances between 2028 and 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, which is meant to cover part of the price gap between fossil marine fuels and sustainable alternatives. Rystad Energy’s analysis shows that, combined with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would reshape the cost ranking of marine fuels in Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels stand to gain the most, while biodiesel made from used cooking oil (UCO) and animal fats – one of today's most widely used marine biofuels – is left out.

The timing matters. From 2026, shipping companies surrender ETS allowances for 100% of their verified emissions in scope, now including methane and nitrous oxide, while FuelEU Maritime requires a steadily tightening cut in the greenhouse-gas intensity of energy used on board. Both regimes rest on the sustainability rules of the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III). For shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers, the question is which fuel pathway the combined rules reward.

SMAP would cover 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with 10 additional percentage points where the feedstock is sourced in the EU. Because support scales with the size of the gap, the most expensive fuels receive the most per tonne, and EU-made e-ammonia could see its entire remaining premium covered (Figure 1). Support is halved on voyages into or out of the EU, and fuels generally must be produced in the EU or in a country with a linked carbon market.

Stacked together, the three instruments push several alternative fuels below the cost of very low sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO) on intra-EU voyages. At 3Q26 prices, bioLNG costs more than twice as much as VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at about half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are counted. Most of that advantage comes from FuelEU Maritime, and bioLNG would already undercut VLSFO without SMAP. Because bioLNG is a drop-in fuel for liquefied natural gas (LNG) engines, this strengthens the business case for LNG dual-fuel ships trading in Europe. RFNBOs receive the most generous treatment of all and, on paper, EU-produced e-ammonia could become the cheapest fuel on intra-EU routes, although very few ships can burn ammonia today and EU production remains small.

The clearest losers are liquid biofuels made from waste oils and fats. UCO and category 1 and 2 animal fats meet every EU sustainability test and earn full credit under both the ETS and FuelEU Maritime, but SMAP supports only advanced biofuels made from feedstocks listed in Annex IX Part A of RED III. Biogas, by contrast, appears eligible regardless of feedstock. The exclusion matters because of how Europe’s biodiesel industry is built. By 2030, crops and waste lipids such as UCO and other waste fats and oils are expected to account for about 96% of the region’s biodiesel and renewable diesel production capacity, leaving only around 2% clearly eligible for support (Figure 2). Aviation’s sustainable fuel mandate is drawing on the same waste lipids, meaning shipping is unlikely to secure much eligible liquid biofuel.

Even for eligible fuels, SMAP is more likely to steer early movers than to drive large volumes. The budget is fixed at around $900 million per year if spread evenly, and claims are cut pro rata when oversubscribed, so owners learn the support per tonne only after the year ends. For bioLNG, mass balance rules also limit supply to bunkers from grid-connected liquefaction in the EU.

The proposal still faces negotiation with the European Parliament and European Council, and the final rules could narrow eligibility or curb overcompensation. Nonetheless, the direction for shipowners is clear: in European trades, fuels that perform well under the ETS, FuelEU Maritime and SMAP together are likely to win. Owners with LNG dual-fuel tonnage and early movers in e-fuels stand to benefit most, while those relying on waste-oil biodiesel should prepare for a widening cost gap.
