title: Titan analysis shows FuelEU pooling propelled liquefied biomethane demand
summary: Titan, part of Molgas, has analysed the role of LNG, liquefied biomethane (LBM/bio-LNG) and e-methane (the methane decarbonisation pathway) in FuelEU Maritime compliance, as well as the performance of...
content:
Titan, part of Molgas, has analysed the role of LNG, liquefied biomethane (LBM/bio-LNG) and e-methane (the methane decarbonisation pathway) in FuelEU Maritime compliance, as well as the performance of the regulation, particularly its pooling mechanism, so far.

The paper models compliance for an 8,000 TEU containership operating a route spanning Rotterdam, Antwerp, Hamburg and Algeciras using approximately 18,000 metric tons of LNG-equivalent fuel annually, all within the scope of FuelEU Maritime. Three scenarios are shown: a fuel oil baseline, grey LNG, and a 30% LBM blend.

The oil-fuelled vessel is in deficit in 2025, and penalty costs grow steeply from ~€2.2M to ~€17M by 2040 as targets tighten. With LNG, the containership generates overcompliance of 11,700 tCO₂eq per year in 2025 and remains compliant through 2035. From 2040, a typical 15% LBM blend restores compliance, and any extra LBM generates surplus pooling value. Introducing a 30% LBM blend can increase that surplus to over 34,000 tCO₂eq annually. That represents ~€3.4M to ~€5.1M per year in gross transferable compliance value.

The figures use FuelEU Maritime’s default well-to-wake emissions factor, covering the fuel’s full lifecycle, together with the published penalty rate of €2,400 per ton VLSFO energy equivalent. Gross pooling values are indicative, based on a market range of €100–150/ tCO₂eq. The net commercial benefit will depend on the market compliance values negotiated and the cost premium of LBM versus fossil LNG. For customers, Titan can model this precisely for each ship and supply scenario.

Grégoire Hartig, Commercial Director at Titan, commented: “Pooling effectively converts over-achieving emissions performance targets into a tradable or allocatable asset. This bridges the market and competition-based nature of maritime transport with the implementation of stringent greenhouse gas regulation. This has, in our view, proven to be a very efficient way to ensure the active participation and alignment of all stakeholders.

“In large part due to ship operators seeking FuelEU Maritime overcompliance, we have already recorded LBM rising from 6.5% to 19.1% of our total delivered volume of methane from 2024 to 2025. LBM prices have been high in 2026 so far, we expect a better second half to the year. Let’s not forget, though, that 2025 has only been the first year where FuelEU pools have been implemented, and that, through iteration, the role of LBM and its impact on compliance values will become clearer.”

Maro Varvate, Commercial Manager at Titan, said: “FuelEU offers a strategic, practical and cost-effective approach to decarbonisation and fleet renewal, which takes into account the lifecycle of maritime asset investment. If ship operators are pooling their own ships, it allows them to target and sequence decarbonisation investments pragmatically, improving selected vessels first while maintaining compliance across their fleet.

“This targeted approach also makes sense from a fuel supply point of view. It allows LNG, and particularly LBM as it continues to scale up, to be efficiently produced and supplied to one ship in one location, and yet the benefits can be shared over the wider shipping service. This also enables demand to incrementally scale up as profits are being made from over-compliant vessels.”

Beyond pooling, the paper argues that the EU’s well-to-tank default emissions factor for LNG is too high. It cites Rystad Energy’s LNG ‘Well-To-Tank Emissions Assessment 2025’ report, where the global well-to-tank emissions intensity of LNG used as bunker fuel in 2024 was shown to be 13.9 g CO2e/MJ (LHV), below the current EU well-to-tank default of 18.5 gCO2e/MJ.

Titan also discusses the journey that the LNG Industry has been on in reducing methane slip and upstream supply chain leakage. It calls on regulators to reward good performance and penalise poor performance, highlighting that the current generic default emissions factor offers almost no compliance or financial incentive for shipowners to choose engine technology with minimal slip and use LNG with lower-emission supply chains.

title: New report reveals China’s key strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks
summary: A Global Maritime Forum report positions China as a leader in "green shipping corridors," linking over 20 initiatives to its ports. However, the report provides scant evidence of immediate, measurable reductions in carbon intensity or a shift away from high-carbon fuels on these routes. Without verifiable deployment of truly zero-emission vessels and significant improvements to existing ships' CII ratings, these corridors risk remaining mere greenwashing rhetoric.
content:
A new report from the Global Maritime Forum reveals that China has quickly become a global leader in green shipping corridors, with nearly one-fifth of the world’s corridor initiatives connecting to a Chinese port.

Launched today at the Global Maritime Forum’s Annual Summit 2026 in Shanghai, ‘Green shipping corridors: How China is re-energising the global movement’ measures China’s progress against the four key building blocks considered crucial to successfully starting up a green corridor. The report finds that China is one of the strongest actors globally in this space, holding strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks.

“The Global Maritime Forum has been measuring global progress on green corridors since 2022, when China was involved in three announced initiatives—now, that number has risen to more than 20,” said Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum. “China’s advancements on green fuel development and efforts around international collaboration could be success factors for these initiatives.”

First introduced in a 2021 report for the Getting to Zero Coalition, the concept of the four building blocks remains a useful tool for benchmarking corridor viability:

• Viable zero-emission fuel and technology pathways: Availability of zero-emission fuels, technologies, and bunkering infrastructure to service zero-emission vessels.

• Cross-value-chain collaboration: Stakeholders committed to decarbonisation and willing to explore new forms of collaboration from both demand and supply sides.

• Enabling policy environment: Policy incentives and regulations that narrow the cost gap and expedite safety measures.

• Customer demand: Conditions need to be in place to mobilise demand for green shipping and scale zero-emission shipping on the corridor.

China’s performance across the first three building blocks is strong; it is an early and cost-competitive producer of green methanol and ammonia, is at the forefront of marine battery development, is highly engaged in cross-value chain collaborations, and is rapidly strengthening its policies related to green hydrogen.

As is the case in many countries, the report reveals that customer demand for China’s zero-emission fuels (the fourth building block) is lagging behind the levels needed to match its potential supply. However, the report outlines multiple opportunities for China to better mobilise demand, including using policy mechanisms to close the cost gap and further advance infrastructure for methanol, ammonia, and battery electric ships.

title: Dual-Fuel Ship Fleet Tops 500 as Industry Investment Passes $200 Billion
summary: The World Shipping Council reports 503 dual-fuel vessels in service and 849 on order, totaling over $200 billion in claimed 'green' investment. However, these 'alternative-fuel-capable' ships frequently operate on conventional, high-carbon fuels like HFO when economically convenient, undermining actual emissions reductions. This greenwashing is further exposed by the concurrent increase in orders for conventionally fueled vessels, clearly prioritizing short-term profits over genuine decarbonization.
content:
The global fleet of dual-fuel containerships and vehicle carriers has surpassed 500 vessels, with shipowners committing more than $200 billion to ships capable of running on alternative fuels, according to new figures from the World Shipping Council (WSC).

The latest WSC Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard shows 503 dual-fuel vessels in service as of September 2026, a 41% increase from 358 a year earlier. Another 849 ships are on order, bringing the combined total to 1,352 vessels.

The figures highlight the scale of investment underway as container lines and vehicle carriers prepare for a transition to lower-emission fuels, even as uncertainty over future environmental regulations continues to cloud the industry’s outlook.

“The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek. “The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions.”

Dual-fuel vessels are designed to operate on conventional marine fuels as well as alternative fuels, giving operators flexibility as new fuel supplies and infrastructure develop. However, their ability to reduce emissions depends heavily on the availability and cost of cleaner fuels.

According to WSC, alternative-fuel-capable vessels now account for 65% of containerships and 97% of vehicle carriers on order, measured by deadweight tonnage. That compares with just 23% across the rest of the global shipping fleet.

Despite that shift, orders for conventionally fueled ships have also increased over the past year as the overall orderbook continues to expand.

The mixed picture comes amid continued uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which would introduce a global marine fuel standard and greenhouse gas pricing mechanism. Adoption of the framework was postponed in October 2025, with negotiations set to resume later this year.

WSC argues that a global regulatory framework is needed to close the cost gap between conventional fuels and renewable and near-zero-emission alternatives while giving shipowners and fuel producers the certainty needed to invest.

Without an international agreement, the industry also faces the prospect of an increasingly fragmented system of regional emissions rules, adding costs and complexity to global shipping.

“Ships ordered today will be operating for decades. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Kramek said.

The IMO is scheduled to hold its next Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting from November 30 to December 3, with a possible resumed session on the Net-Zero Framework on December 4.

“We trust IMO member states can come together to deliver that framework,” Kramek said. “Every delay means increased uncertainty, making the transition harder and costlier for the global economy.”

title: MARPOWER Advances Key Technologies For Maritime Decarbonization
summary: The EU's MARPOWER project touts "decarbonization" through advanced gas turbines for future ships, yet this R&D initiative remains years away from real-world application. After two years, the project reports progress on component designs and a hydrogen-tested combustion chamber, alongside intricate digital twin development for potential efficiency gains. Meanwhile, the global fleet continues to emit millions of tonnes of CO2 annually, demanding immediate action beyond long-term technological promises.
content:
Maritime transport remains one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize due to its high energy requirements, reliance on fossil fuels and the long operational lifetime of vessels. Against this backdrop, the EU-funded MARPOWER project (Efficient zero-emissions gas turbine POWER system for MARitime transport) is developing an advanced gas turbine-based energy conversion system for power generation and cogeneration on board ships, designed to operate with different sustainable fuels while improving overall efficiency.

Two years into the project, the overall cycle and system design has been completed and detailed designs have been developed for its main components. Several critical technologies have also progressed into manufacturing and experimental testing, while the Digital Twin is becoming increasingly detailed. These advances range from optimised compressors and turbines and the successful testing of a combustion chamber prototype with 100% hydrogen to heat recovery technologies, active magnetic bearing systems and increasingly

integrated digital models.

Efficient operation of the MARPOWER system depends in part on the performance of its compressors and turbines. Designs for both the low- and highpressure compressors have now been completed, together with the aerodynamic and cooling design of the high-pressure turbine and the design and optimization of the low-pressure turbine.

Their development has had to take into account several particular characteristics of the MARPOWER architecture. These include its two-shaft configuration, with both spools operating at the same angular speed, and the integration of active magnetic bearings (AMBs), which requires larger clearances to be considered in the aerodynamic design. Fuel flexibility adds another requirement, as operation with different fuels can result in variations in turbine inlet temperature.

The work has also produced dedicated optimisation tools. For the high-pressure turbine, a new procedure was developed to optimise its internal cooling channels. The resulting design was assessed through advanced conjugate heat-transfer simulations and requires a coolant flow rate approximately 15% lower than estimates based on standard literature correlations. The low-pressure turbine has meanwhile been optimised using fully three-dimensional blade shapes tailored to its particular geometry.

With the detailed three-dimensional configurations now available, further work will focus on characterising turbomachinery performance under off-design, transient and fuel-flexible operating conditions.

Developing combustion for fuel flexibility

Fuel flexibility is a central feature of the MARPOWER concept. The system is being developed to accommodate different sustainable and net-zero fuel options, including hydrogen, ammonia, renewable methanol and renewable methane, with limited modifications to the combustion system. The first MARPOWER combustion chamber prototype has been manufactured, instrumented and successfully tested with 100% hydrogen in an atmospheric test rig, following extensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations and the

build-up of the necessary hydrogen supply and distribution infrastructure.

The experimental results, together with further simulations, are now supporting the design of a second prototype. This includes a flexible air distribution system and further geometry optimisations, intended to increase the fuel flexibility of the combustion system.

Making greater use of available heat

Improving the overall efficiency of MARPOWER depends not only on the performance of the gas turbine itself, but also on making greater use of thermal energy available within and downstream of the cycle. A scaled recuperator prototype has been manufactured and assembled and has passed nondestructive testing and pressure testing at 22.3 bar, around 22 times atmospheric pressure. The recuperator recovers heat within the gas turbine cycle. Its 1:100 capacityscale prototype incorporates a new heat-transfer surface geometry, while automated robotic laser welding has been implemented in its manufacture. Preparatory tests have been carried out and final modifications to the test facility are under way ahead of further experimental validation.

The MARPOWER project combines recuperation with a complementary Waste Heat Recovery System to make further use of exhaust heat. The design of this system has been completed, covering the WHR boiler and the associated cycle, including the steam turbine, pump, generator, AMBs and rotor dynamics. Together, these approaches are intended to increase overall efficiency and reduce fuel consumption.

Active magnetic bearings for high-speed machinery

MARPOWER’s high-speed rotating machinery requires bearing and control technologies capable of supporting the rotor while limiting mechanical wear. Active magnetic bearings (AMBs) support the rotor without conventional mechanical contact and allow its position to be actively controlled, making them an important part of the MARPOWER energy conversion system.

A new axial AMB has been designed, manufactured and integrated into an existing flywheel test rig, where initial rotor impact and recovery tests have been successfully conducted. A multiphysics mathematical model combining rotor dynamics, electromagnetics and the thermal behaviour of the AMBs has also been developed, providing a basis for future model-based control strategies that account for temperature-dependent effects.

The project is also addressing the challenge of testing the 2.7 MW rotor system under ship movements. Similarity theory is being used to develop a smaller rotor reproducing the relevant dynamic characteristics of the full-scale system, together with a hydraulically actuated moving platform capable of reproducing surge, pitch and roll. This will allow rotor dynamics and AMB control to be investigated experimentally under representative movements at a manageable scale and compared with the full-scale system.

In parallel, the high-pressure shaft prototype is progressing through mechanical design, Finite Element Analysis, rotor dynamics and AMB modelling, with work continuing towards manufacturing and subsequent experimental validation.

Bringing the technologies together through a Digital Twin

Understanding how the different MARPOWER technologies interact at system level requires their models and data to be brought together. A first calibrated version of the MARPOWER Digital Twin general model has been established around the selected system design point, with increasingly detailed component information being progressively incorporated.

The simulation workflow has been automated to support systematic studies of different operating conditions, including part-load, non-nominal operation and fuel switching. A first system-level sensitivity analysis has also identified parameters with a significant influence on generated power and thermal efficiency, including turbine inlet temperature, ambient temperature and low-pressure compressor efficiency, helping prioritise subsequent parametric studies.

A dedicated AMB sub-model has also been packaged as a Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU), allowing the rotor dynamics and thermodynamic models to exchange information and run together in co-simulation. As experimental data become available from the different technologies, they will progressively be used to refine and cross-validate the Digital Twin.

Next steps: from individual technologies to maritime integration During the second half of the MARPOWER project, work will increasingly move towards further experimental testing, integration and validation under more representative conditions.

Among the most immediate activities are further testing of the combustion chamber and recuperator, manufacture and assembly of the second combustion chamber prototype, further development and testing of the shaft and AMB configurations, and refinement of the Digital Twin using higher-fidelity component models and experimental data.

The project is also entering the stage in which the complete energy conversion system will be assessed in the context of its integration on board ships. Two case studies will consider reference container and cruise vessels, examining basic engine-room arrangements and using digital simulations to assess energy and emissions performance under different operating scenarios.

The vessel studies will also be relevant to the potential integration of MARPOWER technologies into existing ships. This is particularly important given the long operational lifetime of vessels and the technical and economic challenges involved in incorporating new technologies into the existing fleet. Technical performance alone will not determine the potential applicability of the MARPOWER system. Regulatory compliance activities will assess the proposed technologies against applicable safety regulations, standards and engineering practices, including consideration of an Approval in Principle (AiP) and a Technology Qualification Process (TQP), and support their progression towards future certification.

Further work will address safety and risk, maintenance, Life Cycle Assessment and Life Cycle Costing. Together with the vessel studies and technical validation, these activities will provide a broader basis for assessing the integration, safety, environmental performance and economic implications of the complete MARPOWER system.

Building on MARPOWER’s first two years

The results generated during the first half of MARPOWER are also beginning to reach the wider scientific and engineering community. Technical advances from the project have already been presented at relevant international events, including ASME Turbo Expo and IFToMM Rotordynamics 2026. As experimental, modelling and validation activities progress, further results are expected to lead to scientific publications and new conference contributions.

For Professor Jussi Sopanen, MARPOWER Project Coordinator at LUT University, the halfway point marks a transition towards a more integrated phase of the project: “During the first half of MARPOWER, we have advanced the system design, developed key technologies and started generating experimental results. The challenge now is to bring these developments progressively together, extend testing under more representative conditions and generate the evidence needed to assess the complete system and its integration on board ships”.

title: UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape
summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping is already warning against "red tape" in upcoming British maritime fuel standards, citing the perceived administrative burden of FuelEU Maritime, which comes into force in January 2025. Their policy paper, published this week, demands "flexibility" and "realistic emissions targets," a familiar industry lament often preceding attempts to water down effective decarbonization. Such pre-emptive lobbying for less stringent regulation risks delaying tangible progress on carbon intensity reduction and allowing continued reliance on high-carbon fuels.
content:
The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard.

In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January 2025, had imposed a substantially greater administrative workload on shipowners and regulators than initially anticipated.

The 22-page report identifies difficulties with reporting deadlines, fuel certification, emissions calculations and compliance pooling arrangements. Some operators missed deadlines despite meeting their operational obligations, while inconsistencies between verification systems created additional work.

The Chamber wants the UK government to establish a fully tested ship-level monitoring and reporting system before introducing compliance obligations.

It is also pushing for fuel-neutral regulation, realistic emissions targets based on fuel availability and infrastructure readiness, and flexibility for owners and operators to meet their obligations without unnecessary commercial disruption.

Peter Aylott, the Chamber’s director of policy, said the government had an opportunity to learn from the EU’s experience rather than create another regulatory system that increased costs and complexity.

The paper also calls for close alignment with emerging International Maritime Organization requirements to avoid duplicate certification, reporting and verification obligations.

The intervention comes as the Department for Transport prepares to consult on a domestic maritime fuel standard, with the consultation expected later this year.

Britain’s maritime decarbonisation strategy, unveiled in March 2025, targets a 30% reduction in domestic shipping’s lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, rising to 80% by 2040 and zero by 2050, against a 2008 baseline.

The government has identified fuel regulation and emissions pricing as central measures for meeting those targets.

title: Japan’s flawed shipping proposal leaves developing countries adrift
summary: Japan's latest IMO proposal for the Net-Zero Framework critically undermines the 2023 Revised Strategy, risking genuine maritime decarbonization efforts. The plan to scrap the Net-Zero Fund and introduce industry-led "direct contributions" shifts accountability, potentially allowing large shipping lines to direct funds back into their own supply chains rather than global climate solutions. This move weakens incentives for zero-emission energy uptake and deprives developing nations of crucial support, effectively greenlighting continued carbon intensity for some carriers.
content:
A new analysis by Opportunity Green warns governments of the wide-ranging risks posed by Japan’s proposal at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), ahead of adoption negotiations on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) this November and December in London.

Japan’s latest proposal for changes to the NZF would significantly alter the agreed policy architecture, undermining even further the chances of making the 2023 Revised Strategy a reality. The primary changes involve: removing the Net-Zero Fund, the key pillar of “economic measure”; making the purchase of Surplus Units (SUs) the primary mechanism for addressing compliance deficits; and introducing an industry-led “direct contribution” as a global financing mechanism.

Opportunity Green highlights four interconnected risks for IMO member states in this scenario:

1. Scrapping a just and equitable transition: A global IMO Fund is the tool to ensure climate vulnerable developing countries are supported in shipping’s clean transition, which countries committed to under the Revised Strategy. As it stands, the NZF would generate $10-15bn in additional, predictable compliance revenue to help countries meet their needs: investments in zero-emission ship technologies and energy and more resilient trade infrastructure. Removing the Fund also means losing the enforcement mechanism for the Framework.

2. Depriving countries of the power to shape the maritime transition: Replacing the Fund with “direct contributions”, a system where companies are in charge of deciding where revenues are directed, effectively transfers decision-making power to companies. It could result in larger fleet owners paying compliance revenues back into their own supply chains and infrastructure, as opposed towards the needs of the global sector or climate vulnerable developing countries.

3. Weakening incentives for zero-emission energy: Using SUs for compliance would undermine incentives for early uptake of zero-emission energy and fuels, allowing companies to effectively pay to pollute instead of investing in their transition.

4. Undermining emission reduction: Weak incentives for zero-emission energy and fuels would also mean prolonged use of high-emitting fuels such as fossil-based liquefied natural gas (LNG) and biofuels in the industry. This would mean shipping cannot meet the emission reduction targets countries have committed to.

At the upcoming round of negotiations in November and December, countries are urged to retain key principles of the NZF and adopt the agreement in its current form to keep a fighting chance of meeting the IMO Revised Strategy and support states in meeting their international legal obligations on climate change.

Em Fenton, Senior Director at Opportunity Green, said:

“Under Japan’s proposal, countries would be forced to concede the power to shape the global maritime transition to the private sector, with no safeguards or guarantees to deliver justice and equity. It’s like giving up the driving seat and letting big businesses not just hold the wheel but also pick the route. The ones set to lose the most are climate vulnerable and developing countries in the global majority. The Net-Zero Framework as agreed in April last year is the best, fairest and most effective solution on the table that can still drive the clean transition.”

Full Report

title: New study finds shipping pays twice its share to EU ETS: earmarked revenues should triple to help build market for sustainable fuels and technologies
summary: European shipowners are demanding a staggering EUR 30 billion from EU ETS revenues, insisting the proposed Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) fund is inadequate for their "transition." This plea for public subsidy comes despite the sector's substantial profits and ongoing reliance on high-carbon HFO, effectively asking taxpayers to fund their compliance. Regulators must demand rigorous transparency to ensure these billions accelerate genuine decarbonization, rather than subsidizing incremental "greenwashing" projects.
content:
Shipping is responsible for around 10% of EU ETS emissions but pays almost 20% of the ETS bill. Unlike other sectors, it has never received free allowances.

The new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism is a chance to reinvest part of this contribution in shipping’s energy transition. But a new study by European Shipowners | ECSA finds that the Commission’s proposed 110 million allowances cover only a third of what is needed.

SMAP needs at least 330 million allowances (EUR 30 billion) to help create a market for sustainable maritime fuels and technologies, the study finds. For SMAP to meet this objective, this support must cover all sustainable fuels and technologies, including energy efficiency projects, that facilitate the energy transition of shipping.

ES|ECSA calls on the European Parliament and the Council to at least triple the ETS revenues earmarked for SMAP. This is crucial to helping shipping meet FuelEU Maritime’s 2040 target, while helping to create a market for sustainable fuels and technologies that facilitate the energy transition of shipping.

“Shipping pays almost 20% of the total ETS revenues, although it is responsible for 10% of the emissions covered by the ETS. Unlike other sectors, it has never received a single free allowance.

The new ETS mechanism that earmarks part of these revenues offers an opportunity to support shipping’s energy transition. However, the Commission proposal covers only a third of what is needed to help create a market for clean fuels and tech.

title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show
summary: The Monaco Yacht Show, despite its implicit "extreme emissions" title, showcased extravagant superyachts without apparent regard for their significant environmental impact. A "modest" 23.9-meter Zeelander 8, priced at €9.5m and reaching 40 knots, exemplifies the carbon-intensive luxury this sector promotes. This industry's continued focus on opulence over operational transparency and environmental accountability remains a critical oversight for maritime pollution.
content:
Who knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?

To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.

For now, though, I’m boarding my first vessel: a relatively modest Zeelander 8 – 23.9 metres (79ft) long, built in the Netherlands. It has a rather retro look about it, with pleasing curves and a rear end not unlike a Porsche’s. I could imagine James Bond at the wheel. It’s fast too, reaching 40 knots (46mph); I could be in Saint-Tropez in a little over an hour.

Downstairs there’s a huge owner’s cabin, plus a couple of double guest cabins, all en suite, with lots of nice details, such as a cream-coloured leather floor. In the less opulent crew quarters, there’s room for two or three. How much does it cost? This one is not actually for sale – some of the boats here are, others are for charter, some just for show. But I could order one just like it, it would take a year and a half to build and cost me about €9.5m (£8m).

Tempting, certainly, but I need to see a few more before rushing into anything. I can’t help noticing that, compared with some of the others packed into Port Hercules, the Zeelander 8 is a bit … well, small. Is it even a superyacht? There seems to be some debate about how long a yacht has to be to be super – some say 24 metres, others 30.

No question about this one – a Fast50, made by Italian builders Baglietto, with room for 12 guests and a crew of nine. It’s not as fast as the Dutch one, despite the name. Its four engines take it to 30 knots, but that’s actually very quick for a 50 metre boat. Perhaps more importantly, its gross tonnage, referring to internal volume, is 499; a sub-500GT yacht isn’t subject to the more stringent safety and environmental rules under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) that yachts over 500GT are, so they require less frequent surveys and have fewer restrictions on crew size and certification. My favourite features are the large “beach club” (the open deck at the back) and the Jacuzzi right up at the pointy end. Imagine it: sitting with a glass of fizz, in the bubbles, at 30 knots, Céline Dion blasting out … where do I sign?

Oh, again. Not for sale. The first Fast50, fresh from the shipyard, is already sold, but they won’t tell me how much for or who to (superyacht owners can be quite shy). The search continues.

The trouble with superyachting, I’m finding here in Monaco, is that you think you’ve found the perfect vessel, and then you look over there and there’s a bigger, better one. It’s not just me – this is reflected in the Global Order Book, published by Boat International, which tracks construction projects. The 2026 GOB counts the number of yachts over 24 metres under construction globally at 1,093. In 2016, it counted 755 vessels under construction. This year’s figure is actually down 3.95% from last year, but that’s balanced by an increase in average length and gross tonnage. In other words, a few fewer, but they’re getting bigger. New prefixes are required, “mega” and “giga”, but for simplicity’s sake we’ll stick with superyacht. Here at MYS 2026 there are 118 superyachts, with a combined length of 5,508 metres, and a value of €4.5bn.

Despite the sock shame, I’m beginning to feel more comfortable. Most people are friendly. It’s a lovely day on the Côte d’Azur – I’m offered ice-cream, branded fans and straw hats. It’s not just the yachts, there are stands for everything connected. Would I like to come to a wine tasting later “exploring superyacht wine trends”? Of course I would. Am I interested in yachting in Saudi Arabia? Hmmm, maybe next year. There are loads of toys on show – jetskis, eFoils, even submersibles. And if you’re still finding life at sea boring, there’s a portable golf simulator, with cameras and sensors, plus a screen, with hundreds of real courses programmed into it. So after dropping anchor off St Barts you can play a round at St Andrews. It costs €170,000 (£143,000).

And so on to Nixie, built by Lürssen in Germany, owned by co-founder and CEO of Revolut, Nik Storonsky: 102 metres long, with a helipad, glass-bottomed infinity pool, dedicated spa and wellness zone, and a crew of 34, one of whom is busy polishing a stainless steel cleat on the lowest of its decks. Access, though, is “reserved exclusively for direct, potential clients,” says the Lürssen PR. Perhaps they think the average Guardian reader is not in the market to rent a boat the length of a football pitch. Nixie costs €2.4m a week to hire. A lot, I know, but if you split it between the 12 of you …

Anyway, it’s not even the biggest here, which I will be allowed on. First though I pass another – Boardwalk V, only 76.5 metres long and five years old, but this one is for sale, at a discount price! Down €14m, to just €135m. Not including the helicopter. Boardwalk V … it’s ringing a bell. Got it! And now the twin flags on the helicopter’s tail – the American stars and stripes and the tricolore of Italy – make sense. This boat belongs to Tilman Fertitta, billionaire owner of restaurants, hotels, casinos, and the Houston Rockets basketball team, and now Donald Trump’s ambassador to Italy. He made the news in June when hundreds came out to protest after he parked his brand new 117-metre yacht (also named Boardwalk, but without the V) in Venice. He’s got an upgrade – that’s why he’s selling this one.

To be honest there are some proper horrors on show. This one looks like a supersized 80s caravan, that one more like a bridge than a boat, another is bright red – like some kind of firefighting ship. “I don’t understand the clients,” says Rick. “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” Rick is also pretty disparaging about the people who sell these boats, the brokers. “They’re like real estate agents, they say: ‘Look at the master cabin, look at all the light, the big windows,’ it’s all about the interior space.”

Guess what Rick does? Yup, yacht broker. It’s why we’ve changed his name. He also points out something about the way they look. “I don’t know if you’ve heard the analogy, but they look like irons.” As in electric irons, to do the ironing with, and oh my God, he’s so right – that shape, pointy at the bow, then rising and widening as you go aft, with a squared off swim platform … As Rick says, “once you see it, you can’t unsee it.”

In a 2024 study, Oxfam identified 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires and estimated the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. For an average citizen of the world it would take 860 years to produce the same amount.

Oxfam zoomed in further to one family, the Waltons, heirs of the Walmart chain and owners of three superyachts (at this level you’re not talking about the haves and the have-yachts, you’re talking about the have-yachts and the have-lots-of-yachts). They travelled 56,000 nautical miles in a year with a combined carbon footprint of 18,000 tonnes. That’s equivalent to the carbon emissions of about 1,700 Walmart employees.

Superyachts use an awful lot of fuel – some of the bigger ones use more than 500 litres of diesel per hour, releasing CO2 as well as nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide into the atmosphere. The recreational boating sector as a whole – including yachts – produces about 16m tonnes of CO2 annually. It’s not just when they’re going along; at anchor they operate onboard generators to run their “hotel loads” (for air conditioning, stabilisation systems, lighting, galleys, hot tubs, etc) which emit further CO2. In addition, the vessels’ big anchors and chains act like the grim reaper’s scythe on the Posidonia seagrass which grows on the Mediterranean seabed and is a vital habitat for sea life as well as a source of oxygen.

And there are more and more of them. The big increases came in 2022 and 2023 when, as Boat International puts it, “orders soared as UHNWIs sought private holiday cocoons.” UHNWIs, you’ll know, are ultra-high net worth individuals, but why the big boom? Because a superyacht is “the best way to practise social distancing in a very safe and very comfortable way,” says Grégory Salle. Covid was brilliant for the superyacht sector, in other words. Salle is talking to me by video from Lille where he works at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. He’s also author of the thoroughly researched and surprisingly entertaining book Superyachts: Luxury, Tranquility and Ecocide, which has a whole chapter devoted to Posidonia seagrass.

Ecocide is not the superyacht’s only crime. “It has really become the symbol of excessive, unjustifiable wealth,” Salle says. Even though the gap between most of us and the people who have them is virtually unfathomable, “it looks like provocation, especially when all you’re hearing and reading about is crisis, austerity, poverty – including child poverty.”

Superyachts are also a kind of floating paradox that Salle calls “conspicuous seclusion. On the one hand they’re meant to be noticed, they’re massive, you can’t miss them. But at the same time the interior is hidden and of course it can sail away and escape ordinary people.”

Salle uses words and phrases such as “plutocracy”, “oligarchy” and the new “global super-bourgeoisie” about the people who own them, a “transnational capitalist class” who operate outside and above borders and rules. Look at the stern of the superyachts, under the name, and they’re almost all registered in places such as the Cayman Islands, the Marshall Islands, the Isle of Man and Malta – flag states offering, among other benefits, tax neutrality.

It’s hard to hide a superyacht, or ownership of one. We know about Mark Zuckerberg’s 118-metre Launchpad, and Jeff Bezos’s 127-metre Koru, estimated to have cost €444m. Koru caused a stir in 2022, when a historic bridge in Rotterdam, a Dutch national monument, was going to be dismantled in order to let it through. After the uproar its masts were stepped downstream in the end. Koru is actually a sailing yacht, which might sound like a greener way of doing it, but then Bezos also has a 75-metre support vessel, with additional crew accommodation, helipad, submarine, speedboats and cars, that follows Koru around like a loyal dog. Zuckerberg’s got a couple of support vessels too.

Roman Abramovich is another big fan of a yacht. Using leaked documents, Forbes counted 16 belonging to the Russian oligarch. My ship location app tells me that the superest of his fleet – Solaris (140-metres) and Eclipse (162-metres), both registered in the Cook Islands – are now parked in the Sea of Marmara, near Istanbul. When western governments seized Russian oligarchs’ assets after the invasion of Ukraine, Turkey refused to join the sanctions and became a bolt-hole.

Eclipse doesn’t even eclipse everything. The world’s longest superyacht, at 180-metres, is Azzam, launched in 2013 for Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, who died in 2022, but according to Boat International and the Superyacht Fan website, Azzam is still in the family. When you get to this level it’s not always clear who owns a yacht, as they can be held in trusts or shell companies, sometimes across several jurisdictions.

Take Dilbar for example – a little shorter than Azzam but the world’s largest by volume. In June Bloomberg reported that a court in Germany had ruled that sanctions no longer applied to the yacht after finding insufficient evidence that the Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov controls The Sister Trust, which formally owns the vessel.

Or Kosatka, formerly Graceful, the 82-metre yacht seen being escorted through Danish waters by Russian naval vessels in the summer and widely reported to be linked to Vladimir Putin. A bigger, 140-metre yacht, the €620m Scheherazade, which boasts two helipads, anti-drone technology and a cryotherapy room, remains impounded in Italy. Activists working for poisoned Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny believe that one is also owned by Putin.

There is no secret about who owns the aptly named Leviathan, the biggest boat at the Monaco Yacht Show. Co-founder and president of the video game company Valve, Gabe Newell doesn’t just own the 111-metre Leviathan, he also owns the 93-metre support vessel Draak, parked up next door.

I am allowed on to Leviathan and get a brief look around. I’m shown the huge mess area, which Newell and his guests share with the 42 crew. As well as the pool, there’s an outdoor cinema, basketball court, and a huge gaming lounge with consoles and race simulators, open to everyone. The crew are also keen to point out Leviathan’s diesel-electric hybrid propulsion and battery energy storage system. But it still has a 494,000-litre fuel tank. Fill ’er up? Certainly sir, that’ll be roughly a million euros.

It’s not total eco denial at the Monaco Yacht Show however, there’s at least some acknowledgment of environmental impact. I drop in on the Blue Wake awards, “for solutions delivering measurable impact on yachting sustainability”. So there’s a prize for a company using more sustainable materials for yacht interiors. A yacht wins a Blue Wake for having sails, and a marina gets one for planting Posidonia plants.

This is all good news … but actually, when you look at it, it’s not that good. In five years 3,000 sq metres of Posidonia have been restored – sounds impressive, but then by my calculations that’s an area of about 55 metres by 55 metres. The boat with sails? Great, but actually there are fewer sailing boats here than in previous years, the trend is towards power, more and more of it.

It looks like greenwashing, token gestures. I have an Italian friend who calls these superyachts stronzi di mare – turds of the sea. And you know what you can’t do to a turd. There’s no escaping the truth: that they drink fossil fuels like there’s no tomorrow, which there won’t be if they’re allowed to carry on; that there’s no more monstrous symbol of inequality; and that they look like irons.

But before storming off in disgust, maybe I’ll just pop into that wine tasting. In my socks.
